﴿As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved.﴾ Al-Farra' said: what We did to him and to them, of saving him and drowning them, was a reward for one who was disbelieved, and who denied His command, namely Noah, peace be upon him, for they had a blessing which they disbelieved. So the accusative of *jazāʾan* is by way of causation (*ʿilla*). It is also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with an implied verb: meaning, We recompensed them with a recompense.

The majority read *kuffira* in the passive voice, and the one intended is Noah.

It is also said the one intended is God, glorified is He, for they disbelieved in Him and denied His blessing.

Yazid ibn Ruman, Qatada, Mujahid, Humayd, and ʿIsa read *kafara* with a fatḥah on the *kāf* and *fāʾ* in the active voice, meaning: a recompense and punishment for one who disbelieved in God.

﴿And We left it as a sign.﴾ That is, God left the ship as a lesson for those who take heed. It is also said the meaning is: We left this deed which We did to them as a lesson and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its original form is *muddtakir*, then the *tāʾ* was changed to an unpointed *dāl*, then the pointed letter was changed to an unpointed one because of their closeness, and the *dāl* was assimilated into the *dhāl*. The meaning: Is there anyone who admonishes himself and takes heed, who will be warned by this sign and learn from it?

﴿Then how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ That is, My warning.

Al-Farra' said: *al-Inḏār* and *nuḏur* are both verbal nouns, and the interrogative is for magnifying and amazing: that is, they were in a terrifying and wondrous manner which description cannot encompass. It is also said *nuḏur* is the plural of *naḏīr*, and *naḏīr* in the sense of *inḏār* is like *nakīr* in the sense of *inkār*.

﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance.﴾ That is, We made it easy to memorize, and We helped whoever wished to memorize it. It is also said: We prepared it for recollection and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ That is, one who is admonished by its exhortations and takes lessons from its examples.

In the verse is an exhortation to study the Qur'an, to recite it much, and to hasten to learn it. *Muddakir* originally is *mudhtakir*, as mentioned just above.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Anas that "the people of Makkah" asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to show them a sign, so he showed them the moon split in two, until they saw Hira between them.

It is also reported from him through another route, in Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and others, that he said: Then the revelation came: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) into two parts: one part above the mountain, and one part below it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Bear witness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalāʾil* reported from him, who said: I saw the moon split into two halves twice: once in Makkah before the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, one half over Abu Qubays and one half over al-Suwayda. He mentioned that this was the cause of the revelation of the verse.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from him also, who said: I saw the moon split, and I saw the mountain between the two halves of the moon.

He has other chains from him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ — this was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the moon split into two parts: one part beyond the mountain and one part behind it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: O God, bear witness."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, concerning His saying: ﴿and the moon has split﴾, who said: "The moon split while we were in Makkah in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until it became one part on this mountain and one part on this mountain. The people said: Muhammad has bewitched us. A man said: If he has bewitched you, he cannot bewitch all the people."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawāʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman delivered a sermon to us at al-Mada'in. He praised God and extolled Him, then said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.﴾ Behold, the Hour has drawn near. Behold, the moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Behold, the world has announced its parting; today is the training ground, and tomorrow is the race.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying *muhṭiʿīn* (hastening), that it means *nāẓirīn* (looking).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down﴾, that Kathir said: The sky had not rained before that day or after it except from clouds, but the gates of heaven were opened with water, without clouds, on that day. Then the two waters met.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also, concerning ﴿on [a vessel] of planks and nails﴾, that he said: "The planks are the planks of the ship, and the *dusur* are its ribs (*maʿārīḍuhā*) with which the ship is fastened."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also concerning His saying "*dusur*", that he said: "the nails."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "*al-Dasr* is the keel (*kalkal*) of the ship."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from him also concerning His saying: ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾, that he said: "Were it not that God made it easy upon the tongues of human beings, no one among creation could have spoken the speech of God."

Al-Daylami reported from Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ that he said: "Is there anyone who remembers (*mutadhakkir*)?"

This surah is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority of scholars.

Muqatil said: It is Meccan except for three verses, from His words ﴿Or do they say, "We are a host victorious"﴾ up to His words ﴿and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: This is not authentic.

Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Nahhas, and al-Bayhaqi in ad-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed in Makkah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Iqtarabat" (the Hour has drawn near) is called in the Torah "al-Mubayyidah" (the Whitener), it whitens the face of its companion on the day when faces turn white.

Al-Bayhaqi said: This is munkar (rejected).

Ibn al-Durays narrated from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Farwah, traced back to the Prophet: "Whoever recites ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ every two nights, Allah will raise him on the Day of Resurrection with a face like the full moon on the night of the full moon."

Ibn al-Durays narrated something similar from Layth ibn Ma'n, from a shaykh of Hamdan, traced back to the Prophet, and it has already been mentioned that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite Qaf, and Iqtarabat in the Adha and Fitr [prayers]."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His words ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾: that is, it has drawn near. Without doubt, in relation to what remains of the world after the advent of the Muhammadan prophethood compared to what has passed, it has become near.

It may be said that since it is certain to occur without doubt, it is near, for everything that is coming is near. ﴿And the moon has split﴾: that is, the moon has already split. Likewise Hudhayfah recited it with the addition of "qad" (already). The intended splitting is the one that occurred in the days of prophethood as a miracle for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of the majority of the early and later scholars.

Al-Wahidi said: The scholars of tafsir are unanimous on this, except what 'Uthman ibn 'Ata narrated from his father, that he said: The meaning is "it will split," but all the scholars are against this view.

He said: The Hour's drawing near was mentioned together with the splitting of the moon because its splitting is one of the signs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and his prophethood and his time are among the portents of the Hour's drawing near.

Ibn Kaysan said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech: that is, "the moon has split and the Hour has drawn near."

Al-Qurtubi related from al-Hasan the same view as 'Ata's, that it is the splitting that will occur on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the meaning of ﴿and the moon has split﴾ is: the matter has become clear and manifest, and the Arabs use the moon as a proverb for what is clear.

It was also said that the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness away from it and its rising in the midst of it, just as dawn is called falaq (daybreak) because the darkness splits away from it.

Ibn Kathir said: The splitting did occur in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is established in the mutawatir hadiths with sound chains of narration.

He said: This is a matter agreed upon among the scholars, that the splitting of the moon did occur in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it was one of the brilliant miracles.

Al-Zajjaj said: Some people who deviated from the right path claimed, contrary to what the people of knowledge hold, that its interpretation is that the moon will split on the Day of Resurrection.

But the matter is clear from the wording and the consensus of the people of knowledge, because His words ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾ indicate that this happened in the world, not on the Day of Resurrection. End of quote. No one who opposed the majority and said the splitting will occur on the Day of Resurrection has offered anything beyond mere disbelief in its likelihood, saying: "If it had split in the time of prophethood, no one would have remained who did not see it, since it is a sign, and people are equal regarding signs."

It is answered that it is not necessary that everyone see it, neither rationally, nor by revelation, nor by custom. Moreover, it has been transmitted to us by way of mass transmission (tawatur), and this alone removes the disbelief and strikes it in the face of the one who says it.

The conclusion is that if we look to the Book of Allah, it informs us that it has split, and does not inform us that it will split. If we look to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is established in the Sahih and other sources through mass-transmitted chains that it did occur in the days of prophethood. If we look to the statements of the people of knowledge, they have agreed on this, and we do not give attention to the anomaly of one who deviated or to the disbelief of one who disbelieved. Some of what has been reported on this will come, God willing.

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When the moon split, the polytheists said, "Muhammad has bewitched us." So Allah said: ﴿And if they see a sign﴾, meaning the splitting of the moon, ﴿they turn away﴾ from affirming and believing in it, ﴿and say, "Strong, powerful magic, surpassing every magic,"﴾ from their saying istamarra al-shay' (the thing became strong and firm) when it grew powerful and solid. A group of scholars held that the meaning of mustamirr is strong and powerful.

Al-Akhfash said: It is derived from imrar al-habl (twisting the rope), which is the intensity of its twisting, and this was the view of Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas preferred it. From this is the verse of Laqit:

"Until he persisted in evil, which the sincerity of resolve does not adorn, neither feeble nor weak."

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: ﴿continuous magic﴾ means passing away (dhahib), from their saying marra al-shay' and istamarra when it passed away. This was the view of Qatadah, Mujahid and others, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

It was also said that mustamirr means lasting and continuous, from the poet's saying:

"Verily the world is but nights and days, and nothing of ancient things is lasting (mustamirr)."

That is, enduring and abiding. It was also said that mustamirr means false; this was narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah as well.

It was said that some of it resembles the others. It was said that it has passed from the earth to the sky. It was said that it is from marārah (bitterness): one says marra al-shay' became bitter, that is, detestable to them.

In this verse is the greatest proof that the splitting did occur as we have established earlier.

Then He mentioned their denial, saying: ﴿And they denied and followed their desires﴾: that is, they denied the Messenger of Allah and what they witnessed of the power of Allah, and followed their desires and what the accursed Satan made attractive to them. The clause ﴿And every matter is settled﴾ is a new sentence establishing the falsity of what they said of denial and following desires: that is, every matter among affairs reaches an end; good settles with the people of good, and evil settles with the people of evil.

Al-Farra' said: It means the settling of their denial and the settling of the speech of those who affirm, until they know its reality through reward and punishment.

Al-Kalbi said: The meaning is that every matter has a reality; what is of it in this world will become manifest, and what is of it in the Hereafter will be known.

Al-Jumhur read "mustaqirr" with a kasrah on the qaf, and it is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject "kull" (every).

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the genitive, mustaqirrin, as an adjective of amrin (matter). Shaybah read it with a fatha on the qaf, and this reading is reported from Nafi'.

Abu Hatim said: There is no way to justify it. It was said that it has a justification by supposing an omitted genitive construction: that is, "every matter has stability," or "a time of stability," or "a place of stability," taking it as a verbal noun, or an adverb of time, or an adverb of place.

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news that which contains a deterrent﴾: that is, there has certainly come to the disbelievers of Makkah, or to disbelievers in general, of the news, which is the reports of the denying nations recounted to us in the Qur'an, ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾, that is, a restraining, taking it as a mimi verbal noun. One says "zajartuhu" when I forbade him from evil and admonished him. It is also permissible that it be a noun of place, and the meaning is: there came to them that in which there is a place of restraint, that is, it is in itself a place for that. Its original form is "muztajar," and the ta' of the iftiʿal is changed to dal before za', dal and dhal, as established in its proper place. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "muzzajar," with the ta' of iftiʿal changed to za' and the za' assimilated into za'. The "min" in His words "min al-anba'" is partitive, and it and what it governs are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

The nominative of "hikmatun baligha" (perfect wisdom) is either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a substitute for "ma" (a complete substitution of the whole for the whole, or a substitution of inclusion). The meaning is that the Qur'an is wisdom that has reached its utmost, without deficiency or flaw. It was also read in the accusative, taking it as a circumstantial clause from "ma": that is, while what contains a deterrent is perfect wisdom.

﴿So what do warnings avail?﴾ "Ma" may be interrogative or negative: that is, "what thing do warnings avail?" or "warnings have availed nothing." The "fa'" indicates that the failure to avail follows from the coming of perfect wisdom. The word "nudhur" is the plural of nadhir in the sense of the warner, or in the sense of warning as a verbal noun.

Then He commanded him to turn away from them, saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them since the warning did not affect them. This was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿The day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾: "yawma" is in the accusative, either by a supposed verb: that is, "remember," or by "yakhruju" which follows it, or by "fa-ma tughni," with the clause "so turn away from them" being parenthetical, or by "yaqulu al-kafirun" (the disbelievers will say), or by "khushshaʿan" (humbled). The waw was dropped from "yad'u" to follow the pronunciation, and it was written thus in the script, and the ya' was deleted from "al-dai" for lightness, being satisfied with the kasrah. "Al-Da'i" is Israfil, and "al-shay' al-nukur" is the dreadful matter which they deny, considering it immense because no previous covenant had prepared them for its like.

The majority read with a damma on the kaf. Ibn Kathir read with sukun for lightness. Mujahid and Qatadah read with a kasrah on the kaf and a fatha on the ra', in the form of the passive verb.

﴿Humbled their eyes﴾: The majority read "khushshaʿan," the plural of khashi'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read "khashiʿan" in the singular, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And youths whose faces are beautiful, from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd."

Ibn Mas'ud read "khashiʿah." Al-Farra' said: When the adjective precedes a plural, it is permissible to make it masculine, feminine, or plural, meaning broken plural and not sound plural, because that would be a combination of two agents. Like the majority's reading is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Halting there, my companions, their mounts beside me, saying: 'Do not perish from grief, but endure.'"

"Khushshaʿan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yakhruju," or from the pronoun in "'anhum." Humility in the eyes is lowliness and abasement, and humility is attributed to the eyes because honor and humiliation become apparent in them.

﴿They will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾: that is, they will emerge from the graves. The singular of "ajdath" is "jadath," which is the grave. As if they, because of their multitude and the intermingling of some with others, were scattered locusts, that is, dispersed throughout the regions, intermingled with one another.

﴿Hastening toward the caller﴾: "al-ihṭa'" is hastening. That is, their state is that of hastening toward the caller, who is Israfil. From this is the poet's saying:

"In Dijlah is their abode, and indeed I have seen them in Dijlah hastening toward the summons."

That is, hastening toward it.

Al-Dahhak said: "muqbilin" (approaching). Qatadah said: "'amidin" (intending). 'Ikrimah said: "fatihin aadhanahum ila al-sawt" (opening their ears toward the sound). The first is more preferable, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and others.

The clause ﴿The disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day"﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "muhti'in," with the linking pronoun understood, or it is a new sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What will be the case then?"

"ʿasir" means hard and severe. Attributing this statement to the disbelievers is evidence that the day is not severe upon the believers.

Then He mentioned the detail of some of the previously mentioned general reports, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾: that is, they denied their prophet. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His words ﴿so they denied Our servant﴾ explain what came before of the vague denial, and it contains further affirmation and emphasis: that is, they denied Our servant Noah. It was also said the meaning is: the people of Noah denied the messengers, so they denied Our servant Noah by denying the messengers, for he is one of them.

Then He explained that they did not limit themselves to mere denial, saying: ﴿And they said, "Possessed"﴾: that is, they attributed madness to Noah. His words "wa-zdujir" (and he was restrained) are coordinated with "qalu" (they said): that is, he was restrained from the claim of prophethood and from conveying what he was sent with, by various kinds of restraint. The dal is a substitute for the ta' of iftiʿal as mentioned shortly before. It was also said that it is coordinated with "majnun" (possessed): that is, the jinn carried him away and took away his intellect. The first is more preferable.

Mujahid said: It is from the speech of Allah, Who informed about him that he was rebuked and restrained with abuse and with various kinds of harm.

Al-Razi said: This is the more correct view, because the purpose is to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) by mentioning those who came before him.

﴿So he called upon his Lord: "I am overcome, so help [me]."﴾ That is, he called upon his Lord against his people, saying: "I am overpowered by my people, because of their rebellion against obedience and their hindering me from conveying the message." "So help me" means: avenge me against them.

He asked his Lord, glorified is He, for victory over them when he despaired of their response, and knew their rebellion, their obstinacy, and their persistence in misguidance.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, meaning *bi-annī* ("that I...").

Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash read it with a kasrah on the hamzah. This reading is also reported from ʿAsim, with the implied verb *qāla* ("he said") understood, meaning: *fa-qāla* ("so he said").

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what He punished them with, saying: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down.﴾ That is, pouring down with great force. *Al-Hamr* means pouring abundantly. It is said: *hamara al-māʾ wa-l-damʿa yahmuru hamran wa-humūran*, when it becomes abundant. From this is the poet's saying:

*"Let my eyes pour out abundant tears / over the best of those who dwell in Maʿadd and the settled."*

From this is also the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing an eye:

*"A flowing [tear] that the breeze passes over, then it turns / upon it with a pouring, southern downpour."*

The majority read *fataḥnā* with a light (non-doubled) form. Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read it with doubling (tashdīd).

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs.﴾ That is, We made the entire earth gushing springs. The original phrase was *fajjarnā ʿuyūn al-arḍ* ("We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth").

The majority read *fajjarnā* with doubling. Ibn Masʿud, Abu Haywa, and ʿAsim in one narration from him read it without doubling.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: God revealed to the earth that it should bring forth its water, so it gushed out with springs.

﴿So the waters met for a matter already decreed.﴾ That is, the water of the sky and the water of the earth met for a matter already determined concerning them, meaning: in a state that God had ordained and decreed.

Ibn Qutayba related that the meaning is: at a measure in which neither of them exceeded the other, but the water of the sky and the water of the earth were equal.

Qatada said: It was decreed for them, when they disbelieved, that they would drown.

Al-Jahdari read *fa-ltaqā al-māʾān* (the two waters), and al-Hasan read *fa-ltaqā al-māwān*. This reading is reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

﴿And We carried him on [a vessel] of planks and nails.﴾ That is, We carried Noah on a ship made of planks, which are broad boards. *Dusur* (nails): al-Zajjaj said: these are the nails by which the planks are fastened; its singular is *dissār*, and everything that is inserted into something to bind it is a *dusur*. Qatada, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Zayd, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and others said likewise.

Al-Hasan, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and ʿIkrima said: *al-Dasr* is the back of the ship which the waves strike; it was so named because it pushes (*tadsuru*) the water, that is, it repels it, and *al-Dasr* means repelling.

Al-Layth said: *al-Dissār* is a cord with which the planks of the ship are fastened.

Al-Jawhari said in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: *al-Dissār* is the singular of *al-Dasar*, and they are cords with which the planks of the ship are fastened; it is also said they are nails.

﴿Running under Our eyes.﴾ That is, in Our sight and view, and under Our protection, as in His saying: ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37]. It is also said: by Our command; it is also said: by Our revelation; it is also said: by the springs gushing from the earth; it is also said: by the eyes of Our friends among the angels who are charged with protecting it.

﴿As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved.﴾ Al-Farra' said: what We did to him and to them, of saving him and drowning them, was a reward for one who was disbelieved, and who denied His command, namely Noah, peace be upon him, for they had a blessing which they disbelieved. So the accusative of *jazāʾan* is by way of causation (*ʿilla*). It is also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with an implied verb: meaning, We recompensed them with a recompense.

The majority read *kuffira* in the passive voice, and the one intended is Noah.

It is also said the one intended is God, glorified is He, for they disbelieved in Him and denied His blessing.

Yazid ibn Ruman, Qatada, Mujahid, Humayd, and ʿIsa read *kafara* with a fatḥah on the *kāf* and *fāʾ* in the active voice, meaning: a recompense and punishment for one who disbelieved in God.

﴿And We left it as a sign.﴾ That is, God left the ship as a lesson for those who take heed. It is also said the meaning is: We left this deed which We did to them as a lesson and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its original form is *muddtakir*, then the *tāʾ* was changed to an unpointed *dāl*, then the pointed letter was changed to an unpointed one because of their closeness, and the *dāl* was assimilated into the *dhāl*. The meaning: Is there anyone who admonishes himself and takes heed, who will be warned by this sign and learn from it?

﴿Then how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ That is, My warning.

Al-Farra' said: *al-Inḏār* and *nuḏur* are both verbal nouns, and the interrogative is for magnifying and amazing: that is, they were in a terrifying and wondrous manner which description cannot encompass. It is also said *nuḏur* is the plural of *naḏīr*, and *naḏīr* in the sense of *inḏār* is like *nakīr* in the sense of *inkār*.

﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance.﴾ That is, We made it easy to memorize, and We helped whoever wished to memorize it. It is also said: We prepared it for recollection and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ That is, one who is admonished by its exhortations and takes lessons from its examples.

In the verse is an exhortation to study the Qur'an, to recite it much, and to hasten to learn it. *Muddakir* originally is *mudhtakir*, as mentioned just above.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Anas that "the people of Makkah" asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to show them a sign, so he showed them the moon split in two, until they saw Hira between them.

It is also reported from him through another route, in Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and others, that he said: Then the revelation came: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) into two parts: one part above the mountain, and one part below it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Bear witness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalāʾil* reported from him, who said: I saw the moon split into two halves twice: once in Makkah before the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, one half over Abu Qubays and one half over al-Suwayda. He mentioned that this was the cause of the revelation of the verse.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from him also, who said: I saw the moon split, and I saw the mountain between the two halves of the moon.

He has other chains from him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ — this was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the moon split into two parts: one part beyond the mountain and one part behind it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: O God, bear witness."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, concerning His saying: ﴿and the moon has split﴾, who said: "The moon split while we were in Makkah in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until it became one part on this mountain and one part on this mountain. The people said: Muhammad has bewitched us. A man said: If he has bewitched you, he cannot bewitch all the people."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawāʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman delivered a sermon to us at al-Mada'in. He praised God and extolled Him, then said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.﴾ Behold, the Hour has drawn near. Behold, the moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Behold, the world has announced its parting; today is the training ground, and tomorrow is the race.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying *muhṭiʿīn* (hastening), that it means *nāẓirīn* (looking).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down﴾, that Kathir said: The sky had not rained before that day or after it except from clouds, but the gates of heaven were opened with water, without clouds, on that day. Then the two waters met.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also, concerning ﴿on [a vessel] of planks and nails﴾, that he said: "The planks are the planks of the ship, and the *dusur* are its ribs (*maʿārīḍuhā*) with which the ship is fastened."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also concerning His saying "*dusur*", that he said: "the nails."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "*al-Dasr* is the keel (*kalkal*) of the ship."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from him also concerning His saying: ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾, that he said: "Were it not that God made it easy upon the tongues of human beings, no one among creation could have spoken the speech of God."

Al-Daylami reported from Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ that he said: "Is there anyone who remembers (*mutadhakkir*)?"

This surah is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority of scholars.

Muqatil said: It is Meccan except for three verses, from His words ﴿Or do they say, "We are a host victorious"﴾ up to His words ﴿and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: This is not authentic.

Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Nahhas, and al-Bayhaqi in ad-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed in Makkah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Iqtarabat" (the Hour has drawn near) is called in the Torah "al-Mubayyidah" (the Whitener), it whitens the face of its companion on the day when faces turn white.

Al-Bayhaqi said: This is munkar (rejected).

Ibn al-Durays narrated from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Farwah, traced back to the Prophet: "Whoever recites ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ every two nights, Allah will raise him on the Day of Resurrection with a face like the full moon on the night of the full moon."

Ibn al-Durays narrated something similar from Layth ibn Ma'n, from a shaykh of Hamdan, traced back to the Prophet, and it has already been mentioned that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite Qaf, and Iqtarabat in the Adha and Fitr [prayers]."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His words ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾: that is, it has drawn near. Without doubt, in relation to what remains of the world after the advent of the Muhammadan prophethood compared to what has passed, it has become near.

It may be said that since it is certain to occur without doubt, it is near, for everything that is coming is near. ﴿And the moon has split﴾: that is, the moon has already split. Likewise Hudhayfah recited it with the addition of "qad" (already). The intended splitting is the one that occurred in the days of prophethood as a miracle for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of the majority of the early and later scholars.

Al-Wahidi said: The scholars of tafsir are unanimous on this, except what 'Uthman ibn 'Ata narrated from his father, that he said: The meaning is "it will split," but all the scholars are against this view.

He said: The Hour's drawing near was mentioned together with the splitting of the moon because its splitting is one of the signs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and his prophethood and his time are among the portents of the Hour's drawing near.

Ibn Kaysan said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech: that is, "the moon has split and the Hour has drawn near."

Al-Qurtubi related from al-Hasan the same view as 'Ata's, that it is the splitting that will occur on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the meaning of ﴿and the moon has split﴾ is: the matter has become clear and manifest, and the Arabs use the moon as a proverb for what is clear.

It was also said that the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness away from it and its rising in the midst of it, just as dawn is called falaq (daybreak) because the darkness splits away from it.

Ibn Kathir said: The splitting did occur in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is established in the mutawatir hadiths with sound chains of narration.

He said: This is a matter agreed upon among the scholars, that the splitting of the moon did occur in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it was one of the brilliant miracles.

Al-Zajjaj said: Some people who deviated from the right path claimed, contrary to what the people of knowledge hold, that its interpretation is that the moon will split on the Day of Resurrection.

But the matter is clear from the wording and the consensus of the people of knowledge, because His words ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾ indicate that this happened in the world, not on the Day of Resurrection. End of quote. No one who opposed the majority and said the splitting will occur on the Day of Resurrection has offered anything beyond mere disbelief in its likelihood, saying: "If it had split in the time of prophethood, no one would have remained who did not see it, since it is a sign, and people are equal regarding signs."

It is answered that it is not necessary that everyone see it, neither rationally, nor by revelation, nor by custom. Moreover, it has been transmitted to us by way of mass transmission (tawatur), and this alone removes the disbelief and strikes it in the face of the one who says it.

The conclusion is that if we look to the Book of Allah, it informs us that it has split, and does not inform us that it will split. If we look to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is established in the Sahih and other sources through mass-transmitted chains that it did occur in the days of prophethood. If we look to the statements of the people of knowledge, they have agreed on this, and we do not give attention to the anomaly of one who deviated or to the disbelief of one who disbelieved. Some of what has been reported on this will come, God willing.

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When the moon split, the polytheists said, "Muhammad has bewitched us." So Allah said: ﴿And if they see a sign﴾, meaning the splitting of the moon, ﴿they turn away﴾ from affirming and believing in it, ﴿and say, "Strong, powerful magic, surpassing every magic,"﴾ from their saying istamarra al-shay' (the thing became strong and firm) when it grew powerful and solid. A group of scholars held that the meaning of mustamirr is strong and powerful.

Al-Akhfash said: It is derived from imrar al-habl (twisting the rope), which is the intensity of its twisting, and this was the view of Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas preferred it. From this is the verse of Laqit:

"Until he persisted in evil, which the sincerity of resolve does not adorn, neither feeble nor weak."

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: ﴿continuous magic﴾ means passing away (dhahib), from their saying marra al-shay' and istamarra when it passed away. This was the view of Qatadah, Mujahid and others, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

It was also said that mustamirr means lasting and continuous, from the poet's saying:

"Verily the world is but nights and days, and nothing of ancient things is lasting (mustamirr)."

That is, enduring and abiding. It was also said that mustamirr means false; this was narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah as well.

It was said that some of it resembles the others. It was said that it has passed from the earth to the sky. It was said that it is from marārah (bitterness): one says marra al-shay' became bitter, that is, detestable to them.

In this verse is the greatest proof that the splitting did occur as we have established earlier.

Then He mentioned their denial, saying: ﴿And they denied and followed their desires﴾: that is, they denied the Messenger of Allah and what they witnessed of the power of Allah, and followed their desires and what the accursed Satan made attractive to them. The clause ﴿And every matter is settled﴾ is a new sentence establishing the falsity of what they said of denial and following desires: that is, every matter among affairs reaches an end; good settles with the people of good, and evil settles with the people of evil.

Al-Farra' said: It means the settling of their denial and the settling of the speech of those who affirm, until they know its reality through reward and punishment.

Al-Kalbi said: The meaning is that every matter has a reality; what is of it in this world will become manifest, and what is of it in the Hereafter will be known.

Al-Jumhur read "mustaqirr" with a kasrah on the qaf, and it is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject "kull" (every).

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the genitive, mustaqirrin, as an adjective of amrin (matter). Shaybah read it with a fatha on the qaf, and this reading is reported from Nafi'.

Abu Hatim said: There is no way to justify it. It was said that it has a justification by supposing an omitted genitive construction: that is, "every matter has stability," or "a time of stability," or "a place of stability," taking it as a verbal noun, or an adverb of time, or an adverb of place.

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news that which contains a deterrent﴾: that is, there has certainly come to the disbelievers of Makkah, or to disbelievers in general, of the news, which is the reports of the denying nations recounted to us in the Qur'an, ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾, that is, a restraining, taking it as a mimi verbal noun. One says "zajartuhu" when I forbade him from evil and admonished him. It is also permissible that it be a noun of place, and the meaning is: there came to them that in which there is a place of restraint, that is, it is in itself a place for that. Its original form is "muztajar," and the ta' of the iftiʿal is changed to dal before za', dal and dhal, as established in its proper place. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "muzzajar," with the ta' of iftiʿal changed to za' and the za' assimilated into za'. The "min" in His words "min al-anba'" is partitive, and it and what it governs are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

The nominative of "hikmatun baligha" (perfect wisdom) is either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a substitute for "ma" (a complete substitution of the whole for the whole, or a substitution of inclusion). The meaning is that the Qur'an is wisdom that has reached its utmost, without deficiency or flaw. It was also read in the accusative, taking it as a circumstantial clause from "ma": that is, while what contains a deterrent is perfect wisdom.

﴿So what do warnings avail?﴾ "Ma" may be interrogative or negative: that is, "what thing do warnings avail?" or "warnings have availed nothing." The "fa'" indicates that the failure to avail follows from the coming of perfect wisdom. The word "nudhur" is the plural of nadhir in the sense of the warner, or in the sense of warning as a verbal noun.

Then He commanded him to turn away from them, saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them since the warning did not affect them. This was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿The day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾: "yawma" is in the accusative, either by a supposed verb: that is, "remember," or by "yakhruju" which follows it, or by "fa-ma tughni," with the clause "so turn away from them" being parenthetical, or by "yaqulu al-kafirun" (the disbelievers will say), or by "khushshaʿan" (humbled). The waw was dropped from "yad'u" to follow the pronunciation, and it was written thus in the script, and the ya' was deleted from "al-dai" for lightness, being satisfied with the kasrah. "Al-Da'i" is Israfil, and "al-shay' al-nukur" is the dreadful matter which they deny, considering it immense because no previous covenant had prepared them for its like.

The majority read with a damma on the kaf. Ibn Kathir read with sukun for lightness. Mujahid and Qatadah read with a kasrah on the kaf and a fatha on the ra', in the form of the passive verb.

﴿Humbled their eyes﴾: The majority read "khushshaʿan," the plural of khashi'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read "khashiʿan" in the singular, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And youths whose faces are beautiful, from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd."

Ibn Mas'ud read "khashiʿah." Al-Farra' said: When the adjective precedes a plural, it is permissible to make it masculine, feminine, or plural, meaning broken plural and not sound plural, because that would be a combination of two agents. Like the majority's reading is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Halting there, my companions, their mounts beside me, saying: 'Do not perish from grief, but endure.'"

"Khushshaʿan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yakhruju," or from the pronoun in "'anhum." Humility in the eyes is lowliness and abasement, and humility is attributed to the eyes because honor and humiliation become apparent in them.

﴿They will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾: that is, they will emerge from the graves. The singular of "ajdath" is "jadath," which is the grave. As if they, because of their multitude and the intermingling of some with others, were scattered locusts, that is, dispersed throughout the regions, intermingled with one another.

﴿Hastening toward the caller﴾: "al-ihṭa'" is hastening. That is, their state is that of hastening toward the caller, who is Israfil. From this is the poet's saying:

"In Dijlah is their abode, and indeed I have seen them in Dijlah hastening toward the summons."

That is, hastening toward it.

Al-Dahhak said: "muqbilin" (approaching). Qatadah said: "'amidin" (intending). 'Ikrimah said: "fatihin aadhanahum ila al-sawt" (opening their ears toward the sound). The first is more preferable, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and others.

The clause ﴿The disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day"﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "muhti'in," with the linking pronoun understood, or it is a new sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What will be the case then?"

"ʿasir" means hard and severe. Attributing this statement to the disbelievers is evidence that the day is not severe upon the believers.

Then He mentioned the detail of some of the previously mentioned general reports, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾: that is, they denied their prophet. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His words ﴿so they denied Our servant﴾ explain what came before of the vague denial, and it contains further affirmation and emphasis: that is, they denied Our servant Noah. It was also said the meaning is: the people of Noah denied the messengers, so they denied Our servant Noah by denying the messengers, for he is one of them.

Then He explained that they did not limit themselves to mere denial, saying: ﴿And they said, "Possessed"﴾: that is, they attributed madness to Noah. His words "wa-zdujir" (and he was restrained) are coordinated with "qalu" (they said): that is, he was restrained from the claim of prophethood and from conveying what he was sent with, by various kinds of restraint. The dal is a substitute for the ta' of iftiʿal as mentioned shortly before. It was also said that it is coordinated with "majnun" (possessed): that is, the jinn carried him away and took away his intellect. The first is more preferable.

Mujahid said: It is from the speech of Allah, Who informed about him that he was rebuked and restrained with abuse and with various kinds of harm.

Al-Razi said: This is the more correct view, because the purpose is to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) by mentioning those who came before him.

﴿So he called upon his Lord: "I am overcome, so help [me]."﴾ That is, he called upon his Lord against his people, saying: "I am overpowered by my people, because of their rebellion against obedience and their hindering me from conveying the message." "So help me" means: avenge me against them.

He asked his Lord, glorified is He, for victory over them when he despaired of their response, and knew their rebellion, their obstinacy, and their persistence in misguidance.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, meaning *bi-annī* ("that I...").

Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash read it with a kasrah on the hamzah. This reading is also reported from ʿAsim, with the implied verb *qāla* ("he said") understood, meaning: *fa-qāla* ("so he said").

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what He punished them with, saying: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down.﴾ That is, pouring down with great force. *Al-Hamr* means pouring abundantly. It is said: *hamara al-māʾ wa-l-damʿa yahmuru hamran wa-humūran*, when it becomes abundant. From this is the poet's saying:

*"Let my eyes pour out abundant tears / over the best of those who dwell in Maʿadd and the settled."*

From this is also the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing an eye:

*"A flowing [tear] that the breeze passes over, then it turns / upon it with a pouring, southern downpour."*

The majority read *fataḥnā* with a light (non-doubled) form. Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read it with doubling (tashdīd).

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs.﴾ That is, We made the entire earth gushing springs. The original phrase was *fajjarnā ʿuyūn al-arḍ* ("We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth").

The majority read *fajjarnā* with doubling. Ibn Masʿud, Abu Haywa, and ʿAsim in one narration from him read it without doubling.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: God revealed to the earth that it should bring forth its water, so it gushed out with springs.

﴿So the waters met for a matter already decreed.﴾ That is, the water of the sky and the water of the earth met for a matter already determined concerning them, meaning: in a state that God had ordained and decreed.

Ibn Qutayba related that the meaning is: at a measure in which neither of them exceeded the other, but the water of the sky and the water of the earth were equal.

Qatada said: It was decreed for them, when they disbelieved, that they would drown.

Al-Jahdari read *fa-ltaqā al-māʾān* (the two waters), and al-Hasan read *fa-ltaqā al-māwān*. This reading is reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

﴿And We carried him on [a vessel] of planks and nails.﴾ That is, We carried Noah on a ship made of planks, which are broad boards. *Dusur* (nails): al-Zajjaj said: these are the nails by which the planks are fastened; its singular is *dissār*, and everything that is inserted into something to bind it is a *dusur*. Qatada, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Zayd, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and others said likewise.

Al-Hasan, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and ʿIkrima said: *al-Dasr* is the back of the ship which the waves strike; it was so named because it pushes (*tadsuru*) the water, that is, it repels it, and *al-Dasr* means repelling.

Al-Layth said: *al-Dissār* is a cord with which the planks of the ship are fastened.

Al-Jawhari said in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: *al-Dissār* is the singular of *al-Dasar*, and they are cords with which the planks of the ship are fastened; it is also said they are nails.

﴿Running under Our eyes.﴾ That is, in Our sight and view, and under Our protection, as in His saying: ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37]. It is also said: by Our command; it is also said: by Our revelation; it is also said: by the springs gushing from the earth; it is also said: by the eyes of Our friends among the angels who are charged with protecting it.

﴿As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved.﴾ Al-Farra' said: what We did to him and to them, of saving him and drowning them, was a reward for one who was disbelieved, and who denied His command, namely Noah, peace be upon him, for they had a blessing which they disbelieved. So the accusative of *jazāʾan* is by way of causation (*ʿilla*). It is also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with an implied verb: meaning, We recompensed them with a recompense.

The majority read *kuffira* in the passive voice, and the one intended is Noah.

It is also said the one intended is God, glorified is He, for they disbelieved in Him and denied His blessing.

Yazid ibn Ruman, Qatada, Mujahid, Humayd, and ʿIsa read *kafara* with a fatḥah on the *kāf* and *fāʾ* in the active voice, meaning: a recompense and punishment for one who disbelieved in God.

﴿And We left it as a sign.﴾ That is, God left the ship as a lesson for those who take heed. It is also said the meaning is: We left this deed which We did to them as a lesson and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its original form is *muddtakir*, then the *tāʾ* was changed to an unpointed *dāl*, then the pointed letter was changed to an unpointed one because of their closeness, and the *dāl* was assimilated into the *dhāl*. The meaning: Is there anyone who admonishes himself and takes heed, who will be warned by this sign and learn from it?

﴿Then how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ That is, My warning.

Al-Farra' said: *al-Inḏār* and *nuḏur* are both verbal nouns, and the interrogative is for magnifying and amazing: that is, they were in a terrifying and wondrous manner which description cannot encompass. It is also said *nuḏur* is the plural of *naḏīr*, and *naḏīr* in the sense of *inḏār* is like *nakīr* in the sense of *inkār*.

﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance.﴾ That is, We made it easy to memorize, and We helped whoever wished to memorize it. It is also said: We prepared it for recollection and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ That is, one who is admonished by its exhortations and takes lessons from its examples.

In the verse is an exhortation to study the Qur'an, to recite it much, and to hasten to learn it. *Muddakir* originally is *mudhtakir*, as mentioned just above.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Anas that "the people of Makkah" asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to show them a sign, so he showed them the moon split in two, until they saw Hira between them.

It is also reported from him through another route, in Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and others, that he said: Then the revelation came: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) into two parts: one part above the mountain, and one part below it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Bear witness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalāʾil* reported from him, who said: I saw the moon split into two halves twice: once in Makkah before the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, one half over Abu Qubays and one half over al-Suwayda. He mentioned that this was the cause of the revelation of the verse.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from him also, who said: I saw the moon split, and I saw the mountain between the two halves of the moon.

He has other chains from him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ — this was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the moon split into two parts: one part beyond the mountain and one part behind it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: O God, bear witness."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, concerning His saying: ﴿and the moon has split﴾, who said: "The moon split while we were in Makkah in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until it became one part on this mountain and one part on this mountain. The people said: Muhammad has bewitched us. A man said: If he has bewitched you, he cannot bewitch all the people."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawāʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman delivered a sermon to us at al-Mada'in. He praised God and extolled Him, then said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.﴾ Behold, the Hour has drawn near. Behold, the moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Behold, the world has announced its parting; today is the training ground, and tomorrow is the race.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying *muhṭiʿīn* (hastening), that it means *nāẓirīn* (looking).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down﴾, that Kathir said: The sky had not rained before that day or after it except from clouds, but the gates of heaven were opened with water, without clouds, on that day. Then the two waters met.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also, concerning ﴿on [a vessel] of planks and nails﴾, that he said: "The planks are the planks of the ship, and the *dusur* are its ribs (*maʿārīḍuhā*) with which the ship is fastened."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also concerning His saying "*dusur*", that he said: "the nails."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him that he said: "*al-Dasr* is the keel (*kalkal*) of the ship."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from him also concerning His saying: ﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾, that he said: "Were it not that God made it easy upon the tongues of human beings, no one among creation could have spoken the speech of God."

Al-Daylami reported from Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ that he said: "Is there anyone who remembers (*mutadhakkir*)?"

This surah is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority of scholars.

Muqatil said: It is Meccan except for three verses, from His words ﴿Or do they say, "We are a host victorious"﴾ up to His words ﴿and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: This is not authentic.

Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Nahhas, and al-Bayhaqi in ad-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed in Makkah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Iqtarabat" (the Hour has drawn near) is called in the Torah "al-Mubayyidah" (the Whitener), it whitens the face of its companion on the day when faces turn white.

Al-Bayhaqi said: This is munkar (rejected).

Ibn al-Durays narrated from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Farwah, traced back to the Prophet: "Whoever recites ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ every two nights, Allah will raise him on the Day of Resurrection with a face like the full moon on the night of the full moon."

Ibn al-Durays narrated something similar from Layth ibn Ma'n, from a shaykh of Hamdan, traced back to the Prophet, and it has already been mentioned that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite Qaf, and Iqtarabat in the Adha and Fitr [prayers]."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His words ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾: that is, it has drawn near. Without doubt, in relation to what remains of the world after the advent of the Muhammadan prophethood compared to what has passed, it has become near.

It may be said that since it is certain to occur without doubt, it is near, for everything that is coming is near. ﴿And the moon has split﴾: that is, the moon has already split. Likewise Hudhayfah recited it with the addition of "qad" (already). The intended splitting is the one that occurred in the days of prophethood as a miracle for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is the view of the majority of the early and later scholars.

Al-Wahidi said: The scholars of tafsir are unanimous on this, except what 'Uthman ibn 'Ata narrated from his father, that he said: The meaning is "it will split," but all the scholars are against this view.

He said: The Hour's drawing near was mentioned together with the splitting of the moon because its splitting is one of the signs of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and his prophethood and his time are among the portents of the Hour's drawing near.

Ibn Kaysan said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech: that is, "the moon has split and the Hour has drawn near."

Al-Qurtubi related from al-Hasan the same view as 'Ata's, that it is the splitting that will occur on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the meaning of ﴿and the moon has split﴾ is: the matter has become clear and manifest, and the Arabs use the moon as a proverb for what is clear.

It was also said that the splitting of the moon is the splitting of darkness away from it and its rising in the midst of it, just as dawn is called falaq (daybreak) because the darkness splits away from it.

Ibn Kathir said: The splitting did occur in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is established in the mutawatir hadiths with sound chains of narration.

He said: This is a matter agreed upon among the scholars, that the splitting of the moon did occur in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it was one of the brilliant miracles.

Al-Zajjaj said: Some people who deviated from the right path claimed, contrary to what the people of knowledge hold, that its interpretation is that the moon will split on the Day of Resurrection.

But the matter is clear from the wording and the consensus of the people of knowledge, because His words ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾ indicate that this happened in the world, not on the Day of Resurrection. End of quote. No one who opposed the majority and said the splitting will occur on the Day of Resurrection has offered anything beyond mere disbelief in its likelihood, saying: "If it had split in the time of prophethood, no one would have remained who did not see it, since it is a sign, and people are equal regarding signs."

It is answered that it is not necessary that everyone see it, neither rationally, nor by revelation, nor by custom. Moreover, it has been transmitted to us by way of mass transmission (tawatur), and this alone removes the disbelief and strikes it in the face of the one who says it.

The conclusion is that if we look to the Book of Allah, it informs us that it has split, and does not inform us that it will split. If we look to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is established in the Sahih and other sources through mass-transmitted chains that it did occur in the days of prophethood. If we look to the statements of the people of knowledge, they have agreed on this, and we do not give attention to the anomaly of one who deviated or to the disbelief of one who disbelieved. Some of what has been reported on this will come, God willing.

﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾. Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When the moon split, the polytheists said, "Muhammad has bewitched us." So Allah said: ﴿And if they see a sign﴾, meaning the splitting of the moon, ﴿they turn away﴾ from affirming and believing in it, ﴿and say, "Strong, powerful magic, surpassing every magic,"﴾ from their saying istamarra al-shay' (the thing became strong and firm) when it grew powerful and solid. A group of scholars held that the meaning of mustamirr is strong and powerful.

Al-Akhfash said: It is derived from imrar al-habl (twisting the rope), which is the intensity of its twisting, and this was the view of Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak, and al-Nahhas preferred it. From this is the verse of Laqit:

"Until he persisted in evil, which the sincerity of resolve does not adorn, neither feeble nor weak."

Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: ﴿continuous magic﴾ means passing away (dhahib), from their saying marra al-shay' and istamarra when it passed away. This was the view of Qatadah, Mujahid and others, and al-Nahhas preferred it.

It was also said that mustamirr means lasting and continuous, from the poet's saying:

"Verily the world is but nights and days, and nothing of ancient things is lasting (mustamirr)."

That is, enduring and abiding. It was also said that mustamirr means false; this was narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah as well.

It was said that some of it resembles the others. It was said that it has passed from the earth to the sky. It was said that it is from marārah (bitterness): one says marra al-shay' became bitter, that is, detestable to them.

In this verse is the greatest proof that the splitting did occur as we have established earlier.

Then He mentioned their denial, saying: ﴿And they denied and followed their desires﴾: that is, they denied the Messenger of Allah and what they witnessed of the power of Allah, and followed their desires and what the accursed Satan made attractive to them. The clause ﴿And every matter is settled﴾ is a new sentence establishing the falsity of what they said of denial and following desires: that is, every matter among affairs reaches an end; good settles with the people of good, and evil settles with the people of evil.

Al-Farra' said: It means the settling of their denial and the settling of the speech of those who affirm, until they know its reality through reward and punishment.

Al-Kalbi said: The meaning is that every matter has a reality; what is of it in this world will become manifest, and what is of it in the Hereafter will be known.

Al-Jumhur read "mustaqirr" with a kasrah on the qaf, and it is in the nominative as the predicate of the subject "kull" (every).

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the genitive, mustaqirrin, as an adjective of amrin (matter). Shaybah read it with a fatha on the qaf, and this reading is reported from Nafi'.

Abu Hatim said: There is no way to justify it. It was said that it has a justification by supposing an omitted genitive construction: that is, "every matter has stability," or "a time of stability," or "a place of stability," taking it as a verbal noun, or an adverb of time, or an adverb of place.

﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news that which contains a deterrent﴾: that is, there has certainly come to the disbelievers of Makkah, or to disbelievers in general, of the news, which is the reports of the denying nations recounted to us in the Qur'an, ﴿that which contains a deterrent﴾, that is, a restraining, taking it as a mimi verbal noun. One says "zajartuhu" when I forbade him from evil and admonished him. It is also permissible that it be a noun of place, and the meaning is: there came to them that in which there is a place of restraint, that is, it is in itself a place for that. Its original form is "muztajar," and the ta' of the iftiʿal is changed to dal before za', dal and dhal, as established in its proper place. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "muzzajar," with the ta' of iftiʿal changed to za' and the za' assimilated into za'. The "min" in His words "min al-anba'" is partitive, and it and what it governs are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

The nominative of "hikmatun baligha" (perfect wisdom) is either as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a substitute for "ma" (a complete substitution of the whole for the whole, or a substitution of inclusion). The meaning is that the Qur'an is wisdom that has reached its utmost, without deficiency or flaw. It was also read in the accusative, taking it as a circumstantial clause from "ma": that is, while what contains a deterrent is perfect wisdom.

﴿So what do warnings avail?﴾ "Ma" may be interrogative or negative: that is, "what thing do warnings avail?" or "warnings have availed nothing." The "fa'" indicates that the failure to avail follows from the coming of perfect wisdom. The word "nudhur" is the plural of nadhir in the sense of the warner, or in the sense of warning as a verbal noun.

Then He commanded him to turn away from them, saying: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, turn away from them since the warning did not affect them. This was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿The day the caller calls to a terrible thing﴾: "yawma" is in the accusative, either by a supposed verb: that is, "remember," or by "yakhruju" which follows it, or by "fa-ma tughni," with the clause "so turn away from them" being parenthetical, or by "yaqulu al-kafirun" (the disbelievers will say), or by "khushshaʿan" (humbled). The waw was dropped from "yad'u" to follow the pronunciation, and it was written thus in the script, and the ya' was deleted from "al-dai" for lightness, being satisfied with the kasrah. "Al-Da'i" is Israfil, and "al-shay' al-nukur" is the dreadful matter which they deny, considering it immense because no previous covenant had prepared them for its like.

The majority read with a damma on the kaf. Ibn Kathir read with sukun for lightness. Mujahid and Qatadah read with a kasrah on the kaf and a fatha on the ra', in the form of the passive verb.

﴿Humbled their eyes﴾: The majority read "khushshaʿan," the plural of khashi'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read "khashiʿan" in the singular, and from this is the poet's saying:

"And youths whose faces are beautiful, from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'd."

Ibn Mas'ud read "khashiʿah." Al-Farra' said: When the adjective precedes a plural, it is permissible to make it masculine, feminine, or plural, meaning broken plural and not sound plural, because that would be a combination of two agents. Like the majority's reading is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Halting there, my companions, their mounts beside me, saying: 'Do not perish from grief, but endure.'"

"Khushshaʿan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yakhruju," or from the pronoun in "'anhum." Humility in the eyes is lowliness and abasement, and humility is attributed to the eyes because honor and humiliation become apparent in them.

﴿They will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts﴾: that is, they will emerge from the graves. The singular of "ajdath" is "jadath," which is the grave. As if they, because of their multitude and the intermingling of some with others, were scattered locusts, that is, dispersed throughout the regions, intermingled with one another.

﴿Hastening toward the caller﴾: "al-ihṭa'" is hastening. That is, their state is that of hastening toward the caller, who is Israfil. From this is the poet's saying:

"In Dijlah is their abode, and indeed I have seen them in Dijlah hastening toward the summons."

That is, hastening toward it.

Al-Dahhak said: "muqbilin" (approaching). Qatadah said: "'amidin" (intending). 'Ikrimah said: "fatihin aadhanahum ila al-sawt" (opening their ears toward the sound). The first is more preferable, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and others.

The clause ﴿The disbelievers say, "This is a difficult day"﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "muhti'in," with the linking pronoun understood, or it is a new sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What will be the case then?"

"ʿasir" means hard and severe. Attributing this statement to the disbelievers is evidence that the day is not severe upon the believers.

Then He mentioned the detail of some of the previously mentioned general reports, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾: that is, they denied their prophet. In this is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His words ﴿so they denied Our servant﴾ explain what came before of the vague denial, and it contains further affirmation and emphasis: that is, they denied Our servant Noah. It was also said the meaning is: the people of Noah denied the messengers, so they denied Our servant Noah by denying the messengers, for he is one of them.

Then He explained that they did not limit themselves to mere denial, saying: ﴿And they said, "Possessed"﴾: that is, they attributed madness to Noah. His words "wa-zdujir" (and he was restrained) are coordinated with "qalu" (they said): that is, he was restrained from the claim of prophethood and from conveying what he was sent with, by various kinds of restraint. The dal is a substitute for the ta' of iftiʿal as mentioned shortly before. It was also said that it is coordinated with "majnun" (possessed): that is, the jinn carried him away and took away his intellect. The first is more preferable.

Mujahid said: It is from the speech of Allah, Who informed about him that he was rebuked and restrained with abuse and with various kinds of harm.

Al-Razi said: This is the more correct view, because the purpose is to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) by mentioning those who came before him.

﴿So he called upon his Lord: "I am overcome, so help [me]."﴾ That is, he called upon his Lord against his people, saying: "I am overpowered by my people, because of their rebellion against obedience and their hindering me from conveying the message." "So help me" means: avenge me against them.

He asked his Lord, glorified is He, for victory over them when he despaired of their response, and knew their rebellion, their obstinacy, and their persistence in misguidance.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read *annī* with a fatḥah on the hamzah, meaning *bi-annī* ("that I...").

Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash read it with a kasrah on the hamzah. This reading is also reported from ʿAsim, with the implied verb *qāla* ("he said") understood, meaning: *fa-qāla* ("so he said").

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned what He punished them with, saying: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring down.﴾ That is, pouring down with great force. *Al-Hamr* means pouring abundantly. It is said: *hamara al-māʾ wa-l-damʿa yahmuru hamran wa-humūran*, when it becomes abundant. From this is the poet's saying:

*"Let my eyes pour out abundant tears / over the best of those who dwell in Maʿadd and the settled."*

From this is also the saying of Imru' al-Qays describing an eye:

*"A flowing [tear] that the breeze passes over, then it turns / upon it with a pouring, southern downpour."*

The majority read *fataḥnā* with a light (non-doubled) form. Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read it with doubling (tashdīd).

﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs.﴾ That is, We made the entire earth gushing springs. The original phrase was *fajjarnā ʿuyūn al-arḍ* ("We caused the springs of the earth to gush forth").

The majority read *fajjarnā* with doubling. Ibn Masʿud, Abu Haywa, and ʿAsim in one narration from him read it without doubling.

ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: God revealed to the earth that it should bring forth its water, so it gushed out with springs.

﴿So the waters met for a matter already decreed.﴾ That is, the water of the sky and the water of the earth met for a matter already determined concerning them, meaning: in a state that God had ordained and decreed.

Ibn Qutayba related that the meaning is: at a measure in which neither of them exceeded the other, but the water of the sky and the water of the earth were equal.

Qatada said: It was decreed for them, when they disbelieved, that they would drown.

Al-Jahdari read *fa-ltaqā al-māʾān* (the two waters), and al-Hasan read *fa-ltaqā al-māwān*. This reading is reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb.

﴿And We carried him on [a vessel] of planks and nails.﴾ That is, We carried Noah on a ship made of planks, which are broad boards. *Dusur* (nails): al-Zajjaj said: these are the nails by which the planks are fastened; its singular is *dissār*, and everything that is inserted into something to bind it is a *dusur*. Qatada, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Zayd, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and others said likewise.

Al-Hasan, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and ʿIkrima said: *al-Dasr* is the back of the ship which the waves strike; it was so named because it pushes (*tadsuru*) the water, that is, it repels it, and *al-Dasr* means repelling.

Al-Layth said: *al-Dissār* is a cord with which the planks of the ship are fastened.

Al-Jawhari said in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*: *al-Dissār* is the singular of *al-Dasar*, and they are cords with which the planks of the ship are fastened; it is also said they are nails.

﴿Running under Our eyes.﴾ That is, in Our sight and view, and under Our protection, as in His saying: ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37]. It is also said: by Our command; it is also said: by Our revelation; it is also said: by the springs gushing from the earth; it is also said: by the eyes of Our friends among the angels who are charged with protecting it.

﴿As a recompense for one who had been disbelieved.﴾ Al-Farra' said: what We did to him and to them, of saving him and drowning them, was a reward for one who was disbelieved, and who denied His command, namely Noah, peace be upon him, for they had a blessing which they disbelieved. So the accusative of *jazāʾan* is by way of causation (*ʿilla*). It is also said it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) with an implied verb: meaning, We recompensed them with a recompense.

The majority read *kuffira* in the passive voice, and the one intended is Noah.

It is also said the one intended is God, glorified is He, for they disbelieved in Him and denied His blessing.

Yazid ibn Ruman, Qatada, Mujahid, Humayd, and ʿIsa read *kafara* with a fatḥah on the *kāf* and *fāʾ* in the active voice, meaning: a recompense and punishment for one who disbelieved in God.

﴿And We left it as a sign.﴾ That is, God left the ship as a lesson for those who take heed. It is also said the meaning is: We left this deed which We did to them as a lesson and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its original form is *muddtakir*, then the *tāʾ* was changed to an unpointed *dāl*, then the pointed letter was changed to an unpointed one because of their closeness, and the *dāl* was assimilated into the *dhāl*. The meaning: Is there anyone who admonishes himself and takes heed, who will be warned by this sign and learn from it?

﴿Then how was My punishment and My warnings?﴾ That is, My warning.

Al-Farra' said: *al-Inḏār* and *nuḏur* are both verbal nouns, and the interrogative is for magnifying and amazing: that is, they were in a terrifying and wondrous manner which description cannot encompass. It is also said *nuḏur* is the plural of *naḏīr*, and *naḏīr* in the sense of *inḏār* is like *nakīr* in the sense of *inkār*.

﴿And We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance.﴾ That is, We made it easy to memorize, and We helped whoever wished to memorize it. It is also said: We prepared it for recollection and admonition.

﴿So is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ That is, one who is admonished by its exhortations and takes lessons from its examples.

In the verse is an exhortation to study the Qur'an, to recite it much, and to hasten to learn it. *Muddakir* originally is *mudhtakir*, as mentioned just above.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Anas that "the people of Makkah" asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to show them a sign, so he showed them the moon split in two, until they saw Hira between them.

It is also reported from him through another route, in Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and others, that he said: Then the revelation came: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) into two parts: one part above the mountain, and one part below it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Bear witness."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalāʾil* reported from him, who said: I saw the moon split into two halves twice: once in Makkah before the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, one half over Abu Qubays and one half over al-Suwayda. He mentioned that this was the cause of the revelation of the verse.

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from him also, who said: I saw the moon split, and I saw the mountain between the two halves of the moon.

He has other chains from him.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ — this was in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the moon split into two parts: one part beyond the mountain and one part behind it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: O God, bear witness."

Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, concerning His saying: ﴿and the moon has split﴾, who said: "The moon split while we were in Makkah in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until it became one part on this mountain and one part on this mountain. The people said: Muhammad has bewitched us. A man said: If he has bewitched you, he cannot bewitch all the people."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawāʾid al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Abu Nuʿaym reported from ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who said: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman delivered a sermon to us at al-Mada'in. He praised God and extolled Him, then said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.﴾ Behold, the Hour has drawn near. Behold, the moon split in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).
