"Ah, give me to drink before the wailing of the mourners, and before the agitation of the soul within the ribs, and before tomorrow, O woe to my soul over tomorrow, when my companions depart and I am not returning."

The majority read "sayaʿlamūna" with the yāʾ (third person), as a report from God, glorified is He, to Ṣāliḥ about the occurrence of the punishment upon them after a period.

Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza read it with the tāʾ (second person), as an address from Ṣāliḥ to his people.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾ is a resumptive new sentence explaining what was previously stated in summary of the threat: that is, indeed We are bringing her out from the rock according to what they proposed. ﴿As a trial for them﴾ that is, a test and examination. The accusative of "fitna" is by way of causation (ʿilla). "So watch them" means: wait and see what they do, and be patient over what harm reaches you from them.

﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them﴾ that is, between Thamūd and the she-camel: a day for her, and a day for them, as in His saying: ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 155]. He said "nabbi'hum" with the pronoun for rational beings, by way of precedence (taghlīb). ﴿Every drink shall be attended.﴾ "Shirb" with a kasra on the shīn means the allotted share of water. The meaning of "muḥtaḍar" (attended) is that the one entitled to it attends it: so the she-camel attends it on one day, and they attend it on another day.

Mujahid said: Thamūd would come to the water on their turn day, and drink, and they would come on her turn day and milk her.

The majority read "qisma" with a kasra on the qāf, in the sense of "maqsūm" (allotted). Abu ʿAmr, in a transmission from him, read it with a fatḥa.

﴿Then they called their companion﴾ that is, Thamūd called their companion, who was Qidār ibn Sālif, the hamstringer of the she-camel, urging him to hamstring her. ﴿So he took it in hand and hamstrung her.﴾ That is, he took hold of the she-camel and hamstrung her; or he dared to undertake the means of hamstringing and so hamstrung her. "Taʿāṭā" means taking hold of a thing with effort.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: He lay in ambush for her beneath a tree on her path, and shot her with an arrow which pierced the muscle of her leg; then he attacked her with the sword, cut her hamstring, and then slaughtered her.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He explained the punishment which He had mentioned in summary, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry,﴾ ʿAṭāʾ said: He means the cry of Gabriel. Its explanation has passed in the surah Hūd and in al-Aʿrāf. ﴿So they became like the crushed remains of a fence-builder's enclosure.﴾ The majority read "al-muḥtaẓir" with a kasra on the ẓāʾ. "Hashīm" means the debris and dried part of trees; "al-muḥtaẓir" is the owner of an enclosure, the one who makes for his sheep an enclosure to protect them from the cold wind. It is said: "iḥtaẓara ʿalā ghanamihi" when he gathered trees and placed some of them upon others.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-muḥtaẓir" is the one who builds the enclosure.

Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Abu al-ʿĀliya read it with a fatḥa on the ẓāʾ: that is, like the crushed remains of the enclosure. So whoever reads with a kasra intends the agent of the enclosing; whoever reads with a fatḥa intends the enclosure, which is a "faʿīla" in the sense of "mafʿūla" (passive). The meaning of the verse is that they became like trees which dry out in the enclosure and which the sheep trample after they have fallen. From this is the poet's saying:

"Its dust raised by them like the smoke of a fire, which blazes in an old dried-up thorn-bush."

Qatāda said: It refers to the crumbling, burnt bones.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: It is the dust scattered from the walls on a windy day.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: It is what scatters from the enclosure when you strike it with sticks.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs call everything that was moist and then dried "hashīm," and from this is the poet's saying:

"You see the carcasses of the riding camels on both sides, as if their bones were dry wood of hashīm."

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the people of Lot that they denied the messengers of God, just as others had denied them, and said: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings.﴾ The explanation of "nudhur" has passed shortly before.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-ḥāṣib" is the fierce wind which stirs up pebbles. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Thus said al-Zajjāj, al-Akhfash, and others.

It is the form "tafāʿalū" from "mirya," which means doubt.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wednesday is a day of continuous ill omen." Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him through another chain, as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ) report.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded it from Ali as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from Anas as a marfu' report, and in it: "It was said: 'How is that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Allah drowned Pharaoh and his people in it, and destroyed 'Ad and Thamud in it.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from them (Ibn Abbas and others), regarding ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees﴾, that he said: "The roots of the palm trees, uprooted." He said: "Uprooted."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him, also regarding the verse, that he said: "The trunks of the dark palm trees."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, regarding "and a madness (su'ur)", that he said: "Misery."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, that he said, regarding ﴿like the crushed stubble of a pen-builder﴾: "Like the burnt branches of trees used as enclosures."

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, also, regarding the verse, that he said: "Like burnt bones."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him that he said: "Like grass that is eaten by sheep."

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind,﴾ this clause explains what was previously stated in summary of the punishment. "Ṣarṣar" means intense cold: that is, a wind of intense cold. It has also been said that "ṣarṣar" means intense sound. Its explanation has already passed in the surah Ḥā Mīm (al-Sajda). ﴿On a day of continuous ill omen,﴾ that is, a day of constant misfortune, whose ill fortune persisted over them. They used to consider that day ominous.

Al-Zajjaj said: It has been said that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿a day of ill omen﴾ with the noun "yawm" in construct with "naḥs," and with the ḥāʾ sukūn (unvocalized). This is either the construction of a described noun with its description (iḍāfat al-mawṣūf ilā al-ṣifa), or it is by presuming an omitted noun, that is: "on the day of the punishment of an ill omen."

Al-Ḥasan read "yawmin" with tanwīn, so that "naḥsin" is its attribute (ṣifa).

Hārūn read it with a kasra on the ḥāʾ.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That day was bitter for them.

Likewise al-Kisāʾī narrated from some people that they said: it is from "marāra" (bitterness). It has also been said that it is from "mirra" meaning strength: that is, on a day of powerful, firmly established ill omen, like a thing tightly twisted that cannot be undone. The apparent meaning is that it is from "istimrār" (continuance), not from "marāra" nor from "mirra": that is, the punishment continued over them on that day until it destroyed them, and its destruction encompassed their great and small alike.

The clause ﴿uprooting people﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), either as an attribute of "rīḥan" or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. It is also permissible that it is a resumptive new clause (isti'nāf): that is, it uproots them from the earth from beneath their feet, like the uprooting of a palm tree from its root.

Mujahid said: It would uproot them from the earth and then hurl them upon their heads, breaking their necks and separating their heads from their bodies. It has also been said: it uproots the people from their houses. It has also been said: from their graves, because they had dug trenches and entered them.

﴿As if they were trunks of hollowed palm trees.﴾ "Aʿjāz" is the plural of "ʿajuz," which is the rear part of a thing. "Munqaʿir" means uprooted, torn from its root. It is said: "qaʿʿartu al-nakhla" when I uprooted the palm tree from its root until it falls. He likened them in the height of their statures, when the wind felled them and cast them on their faces, to fallen palm trees on the ground which have no heads; because the wind first tore off their heads, then overturned them on their faces. The masculine form "munqaʿir" with "aʿjāz nakhl," which is feminine, is in consideration of the wording; it is also permissible to make it feminine in consideration of the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. Al-Mubarrad said: Whatever comes to you of this type, if you wish, you may refer it to the wording by using the masculine, or to the meaning by using the feminine.

It has been said that "nakhl" and "nakhīl" may be treated as masculine or feminine.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has been given shortly before. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾

It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun meaning "warning": that is, they denied the warning with which they were warned. Their denial of their messenger, who was Ṣāliḥ, was a denial of (all) messengers, because whoever denies one of the prophets has denied all of them, since they agree on the call to the universal principles of the laws.

﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, how could we follow a human being of our own kind, alone, with no one following him in what he calls to?

The majority read "basharan" with a naṣb (accusative), by way of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with the object pronoun): that is, "Shall we follow a single human?"

It is narrated from Abu al-Simāk that he read "basharun" with raf and "wāḥidan" with naṣb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿Indeed, then we would be in error,﴾ that is: indeed, if we followed him we would be in mistake, going astray from the truth and in "suʿur": that is, torment, hardship, and distress. Thus said al-Farrāʾ and others.

Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of "saʿīr," which is the flame of fire; and "suʿur" is madness, for it goes, such and such, due to what he burns with of heat.

Mujahid said: "suʿur" means: and distance from the truth.

Al-Suddī said: in burning. It has also been said that what is meant here is madness, from their saying: "a she-camel that is maswūra," meaning as if she were mad from the intensity of her vigor. From this is the poet's saying describing a she-camel:

Then they repeated the denial and the disbelief, and said: 25 – ﴿Has the message been cast upon him from among us?﴾ That is: how was he singled out from among us for revelation and prophethood, when among us is one more deserving of that than him?

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, regarding "and a madness (su'ur)", that he said: "Misery."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, that he said, regarding ﴿like the crushed stubble of a pen-builder﴾: "Like the burnt branches of trees used as enclosures."

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, also, regarding the verse, that he said: "Like burnt bones."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him that he said: "Like grass that is eaten by sheep."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The people of ʿĀd denied,﴾ they are the people of ʿĀd. ﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ That is: listen to how My punishment befell them and how My warning (to them) was. "Nudhur" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "warning (indhār)," as its verification has already passed. The interrogative is for expressing awe and magnitude.

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind,﴾ this clause explains what was previously stated in summary of the punishment. "Ṣarṣar" means intense cold: that is, a wind of intense cold. It has also been said that "ṣarṣar" means intense sound. Its explanation has already passed in the surah Ḥā Mīm (al-Sajda). ﴿On a day of continuous ill omen,﴾ that is, a day of constant misfortune, whose ill fortune persisted over them. They used to consider that day ominous.

Al-Zajjaj said: It has been said that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿a day of ill omen﴾ with the noun "yawm" in construct with "naḥs," and with the ḥāʾ sukūn (unvocalized). This is either the construction of a described noun with its description (iḍāfat al-mawṣūf ilā al-ṣifa), or it is by presuming an omitted noun, that is: "on the day of the punishment of an ill omen."

Al-Ḥasan read "yawmin" with tanwīn, so that "naḥsin" is its attribute (ṣifa).

Hārūn read it with a kasra on the ḥāʾ.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That day was bitter for them.

Likewise al-Kisāʾī narrated from some people that they said: it is from "marāra" (bitterness). It has also been said that it is from "mirra" meaning strength: that is, on a day of powerful, firmly established ill omen, like a thing tightly twisted that cannot be undone. The apparent meaning is that it is from "istimrār" (continuance), not from "marāra" nor from "mirra": that is, the punishment continued over them on that day until it destroyed them, and its destruction encompassed their great and small alike.

The clause ﴿uprooting people﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), either as an attribute of "rīḥan" or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. It is also permissible that it is a resumptive new clause (isti'nāf): that is, it uproots them from the earth from beneath their feet, like the uprooting of a palm tree from its root.

Mujahid said: It would uproot them from the earth and then hurl them upon their heads, breaking their necks and separating their heads from their bodies. It has also been said: it uproots the people from their houses. It has also been said: from their graves, because they had dug trenches and entered them.

﴿As if they were trunks of hollowed palm trees.﴾ "Aʿjāz" is the plural of "ʿajuz," which is the rear part of a thing. "Munqaʿir" means uprooted, torn from its root. It is said: "qaʿʿartu al-nakhla" when I uprooted the palm tree from its root until it falls. He likened them in the height of their statures, when the wind felled them and cast them on their faces, to fallen palm trees on the ground which have no heads; because the wind first tore off their heads, then overturned them on their faces. The masculine form "munqaʿir" with "aʿjāz nakhl," which is feminine, is in consideration of the wording; it is also permissible to make it feminine in consideration of the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. Al-Mubarrad said: Whatever comes to you of this type, if you wish, you may refer it to the wording by using the masculine, or to the meaning by using the feminine.

It has been said that "nakhl" and "nakhīl" may be treated as masculine or feminine.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has been given shortly before. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the denial of ʿĀd, He followed it with the denial of Thamūd, and said: ﴿Thamūd denied the warnings.﴾ It is permissible that it is the plural of "nadhīr" (warner): that is, they denied the messengers sent to them. It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun meaning "warning": that is, they denied the warning with which they were warned. Their denial of their messenger, who was Ṣāliḥ, was a denial of (all) messengers, because whoever denies one of the prophets has denied all of them, since they agree on the call to the universal principles of the laws.

﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, how could we follow a human being of our own kind, alone, with no one following him in what he calls to?

The majority read "basharan" with a naṣb (accusative), by way of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with the object pronoun): that is, "Shall we follow a single human?"

Abu al-Simāk, al-Dānī, Abu al-Ashhab, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read it with a raf (nominative) by way of ibtidāʾ (the nominal sentence beginning): "wāḥidan" is its attribute, and "nattabiʿuhu" is its predicate.

It is narrated from Abu al-Simāk that he read "basharun" with raf and "wāḥidan" with naṣb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿Indeed, then we would be in error,﴾ that is: indeed, if we followed him we would be in mistake, going astray from the truth and in "suʿur": that is, torment, hardship, and distress. Thus said al-Farrāʾ and others.

Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of "saʿīr," which is the flame of fire; and "suʿur" is madness, for it goes, such and such, due to what he burns with of heat.

Mujahid said: "suʿur" means: and distance from the truth.

Al-Suddī said: in burning. It has also been said that what is meant here is madness, from their saying: "a she-camel that is maswūra," meaning as if she were mad from the intensity of her vigor. From this is the poet's saying describing a she-camel:

"You imagine in her madness when the madness shakes her, a gait and a rhythm of travel that is tiring."

Then they repeated the denial and the disbelief, and said: 25 – ﴿Has the message been cast upon him from among us?﴾ That is: how was he singled out from among us for revelation and prophethood, when among us is one more deserving of that than him?

Then they turned away from denial and moved on to a firm assertion that he was a liar and insolent, and said: ﴿Rather, he is a liar, insolent.﴾ "Al-Ashar" means exuberance and vigor, or arrogance and haughtiness. Explaining it as arrogance and haughtiness is more fitting to the context. From this is the poet's saying:

"You became arrogant by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, and before that you did not know who conquered the villages."

The majority read "ushira" in the pattern of "fariḥa" (ushira). Abu Qilāba and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a fatḥa on the shīn and shadda on the rāʾ, as an elative form (ism tafḍīl). Al-Kisāʾī transmitted from Mujahid that he read it with a ḍamma on the shīn and a fatḥa on the hamza.

Then He, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent.﴾ What is meant by "tomorrow" is the time of the descent of the punishment upon them in this world, or the Day of Resurrection, following the custom of people in expressing the future matter by "tomorrow," even if it is distant, as in their saying: "Indeed, with today is tomorrow," and as in the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:

"For death in it are arrows that never miss; whoever has not died today will die tomorrow."

From this is the saying of Abu al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

"Ah, give me to drink before the wailing of the mourners, and before the agitation of the soul within the ribs, and before tomorrow, O woe to my soul over tomorrow, when my companions depart and I am not returning."

The majority read "sayaʿlamūna" with the yāʾ (third person), as a report from God, glorified is He, to Ṣāliḥ about the occurrence of the punishment upon them after a period.

Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza read it with the tāʾ (second person), as an address from Ṣāliḥ to his people.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾ is a resumptive new sentence explaining what was previously stated in summary of the threat: that is, indeed We are bringing her out from the rock according to what they proposed. ﴿As a trial for them﴾ that is, a test and examination. The accusative of "fitna" is by way of causation (ʿilla). "So watch them" means: wait and see what they do, and be patient over what harm reaches you from them.

﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them﴾ that is, between Thamūd and the she-camel: a day for her, and a day for them, as in His saying: ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 155]. He said "nabbi'hum" with the pronoun for rational beings, by way of precedence (taghlīb). ﴿Every drink shall be attended.﴾ "Shirb" with a kasra on the shīn means the allotted share of water. The meaning of "muḥtaḍar" (attended) is that the one entitled to it attends it: so the she-camel attends it on one day, and they attend it on another day.

Mujahid said: Thamūd would come to the water on their turn day, and drink, and they would come on her turn day and milk her.

The majority read "qisma" with a kasra on the qāf, in the sense of "maqsūm" (allotted). Abu ʿAmr, in a transmission from him, read it with a fatḥa.

﴿Then they called their companion﴾ that is, Thamūd called their companion, who was Qidār ibn Sālif, the hamstringer of the she-camel, urging him to hamstring her. ﴿So he took it in hand and hamstrung her.﴾ That is, he took hold of the she-camel and hamstrung her; or he dared to undertake the means of hamstringing and so hamstrung her. "Taʿāṭā" means taking hold of a thing with effort.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: He lay in ambush for her beneath a tree on her path, and shot her with an arrow which pierced the muscle of her leg; then he attacked her with the sword, cut her hamstring, and then slaughtered her.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He explained the punishment which He had mentioned in summary, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry,﴾ ʿAṭāʾ said: He means the cry of Gabriel. Its explanation has passed in the surah Hūd and in al-Aʿrāf. ﴿So they became like the crushed remains of a fence-builder's enclosure.﴾ The majority read "al-muḥtaẓir" with a kasra on the ẓāʾ. "Hashīm" means the debris and dried part of trees; "al-muḥtaẓir" is the owner of an enclosure, the one who makes for his sheep an enclosure to protect them from the cold wind. It is said: "iḥtaẓara ʿalā ghanamihi" when he gathered trees and placed some of them upon others.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-muḥtaẓir" is the one who builds the enclosure.

Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Abu al-ʿĀliya read it with a fatḥa on the ẓāʾ: that is, like the crushed remains of the enclosure. So whoever reads with a kasra intends the agent of the enclosing; whoever reads with a fatḥa intends the enclosure, which is a "faʿīla" in the sense of "mafʿūla" (passive). The meaning of the verse is that they became like trees which dry out in the enclosure and which the sheep trample after they have fallen. From this is the poet's saying:

"Its dust raised by them like the smoke of a fire, which blazes in an old dried-up thorn-bush."

Qatāda said: It refers to the crumbling, burnt bones.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: It is the dust scattered from the walls on a windy day.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: It is what scatters from the enclosure when you strike it with sticks.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs call everything that was moist and then dried "hashīm," and from this is the poet's saying:

"You see the carcasses of the riding camels on both sides, as if their bones were dry wood of hashīm."

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the people of Lot that they denied the messengers of God, just as others had denied them, and said: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings.﴾ The explanation of "nudhur" has passed shortly before.

Then He, glorified is He, [p. 1431] explained what He punished them with, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a stone-laden storm﴾ that is, a wind which pelts them with pebbles, which are small stones.

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "al-ḥāṣib" is stones carried by the wind.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-ḥāṣib" is the fierce wind which stirs up pebbles. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with a storm like cotton-tufts scattered."

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾: We delivered them at dawn. That refers to Lot and those who followed him. "Saḥar" is the last part of the night. It has also been said that in the language of the Arabs it is the mixing of the darkness of the night with the whiteness of the beginning of the day. "Saḥar" is treated as indeterminate (and so not diptote) because it is an indefinite noun, not intending a specific dawn of a particular night; had he intended a specific one, it would have been diptote (not taking tanwīn).

Thus said al-Zajjāj, al-Akhfash, and others.

The accusative of ﴿a blessing from Us﴾ is by way of causation or as a verbal noun: that is, a favor from Us upon Lot and those who followed him. ﴿Thus do We reward those who give thanks﴾ that is, in the same manner of that reward We reward whoever gives thanks for Our blessing and does not disbelieve it.

﴿And he had already warned them of Our seizure﴾ that is, Lot warned his people of God's seizure against them, which is His severe punishment and far-reaching retribution. ﴿But they disputed about the warnings﴾ that is, they doubted the warning and did not believe him. It is the form "tafāʿalū" from "mirya," which means doubt.

﴿And they had sought to seduce him away from his guests﴾ that is, they wanted from him to let them have those who came to him from among the angels, so that they might commit lewdness with them, as is their habit. It is said: "rāwadtuhu ʿan kadhā" meaning "murāwada" and "riwād": I sought it from him; and "rāda al-kalām yarūduhu rawdan" meaning he sought it. The explanation of "murāwada" has been given in full in the surah Hūd. ﴿So We blinded their eyes﴾ that is, We made their eyes wiped smooth, with no slit visible, as the wind wipes out markers by blowing dust over them. It has also been said: God removed the light of their sight while their eyes remained in their form. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God wiped their eyes so they did not see the messengers, and so they returned. ﴿So taste My punishment and My warning﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

﴿And there came upon them in the morning a settled punishment﴾ that is, a punishment settled upon them, descending over them, not leaving them nor departing from them, came upon them at dawn.

Muqātil said: The punishment settled upon them at dawn. "Bukra" is not diptote, because it was not intended as a specific time, as was previously explained in "bi-saḥar."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ The tafsir (explanation of the Qur'an) of this has already been given in this surah. Perhaps the purpose of repeating the statement about the Qur'an being made easy for remembrance in this surah is to draw attention to the fact that it is a great favour, and no one should neglect to be grateful for it.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾, that he said: "Cold." ﴿On a day of ill omen﴾, he said: "Days of hardship."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wednesday is a day of continuous ill omen." Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him through another chain, as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ) report.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded it from Ali as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from Anas as a marfu' report, and in it: "It was said: 'How is that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Allah drowned Pharaoh and his people in it, and destroyed 'Ad and Thamud in it.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib recorded, with a chain (sanad) which al-Suyuti described as weak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The last Wednesday of the month is a day of continuous ill omen."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from them (Ibn Abbas and others), regarding ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees﴾, that he said: "The roots of the palm trees, uprooted." He said: "Uprooted."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him, also regarding the verse, that he said: "The trunks of the dark palm trees."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, regarding "and a madness (su'ur)", that he said: "Misery."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, that he said, regarding ﴿like the crushed stubble of a pen-builder﴾: "Like the burnt branches of trees used as enclosures."

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, also, regarding the verse, that he said: "Like burnt bones."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him that he said: "Like grass that is eaten by sheep."

He said "nabbi'hum" with the pronoun for rational beings, by way of precedence (taghlīb). ﴿Every drink shall be attended.﴾ "Shirb" with a kasra on the shīn means the allotted share of water. The meaning of "muḥtaḍar" (attended) is that the one entitled to it attends it: so the she-camel attends it on one day, and they attend it on another day.

Mujahid said: Thamūd would come to the water on their turn day, and drink, and they would come on her turn day and milk her.

The majority read "qisma" with a kasra on the qāf, in the sense of "maqsūm" (allotted). Abu ʿAmr, in a transmission from him, read it with a fatḥa.

﴿Then they called their companion﴾ that is, Thamūd called their companion, who was Qidār ibn Sālif, the hamstringer of the she-camel, urging him to hamstring her. ﴿So he took it in hand and hamstrung her.﴾ That is, he took hold of the she-camel and hamstrung her; or he dared to undertake the means of hamstringing and so hamstrung her. "Taʿāṭā" means taking hold of a thing with effort.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: He lay in ambush for her beneath a tree on her path, and shot her with an arrow which pierced the muscle of her leg; then he attacked her with the sword, cut her hamstring, and then slaughtered her.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He explained the punishment which He had mentioned in summary, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry,﴾ ʿAṭāʾ said: He means the cry of Gabriel. Its explanation has passed in the surah Hūd and in al-Aʿrāf. ﴿So they became like the crushed remains of a fence-builder's enclosure.﴾ The majority read "al-muḥtaẓir" with a kasra on the ẓāʾ. "Hashīm" means the debris and dried part of trees; "al-muḥtaẓir" is the owner of an enclosure, the one who makes for his sheep an enclosure to protect them from the cold wind. It is said: "iḥtaẓara ʿalā ghanamihi" when he gathered trees and placed some of them upon others.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-muḥtaẓir" is the one who builds the enclosure.

Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Abu al-ʿĀliya read it with a fatḥa on the ẓāʾ: that is, like the crushed remains of the enclosure. So whoever reads with a kasra intends the agent of the enclosing; whoever reads with a fatḥa intends the enclosure, which is a "faʿīla" in the sense of "mafʿūla" (passive). The meaning of the verse is that they became like trees which dry out in the enclosure and which the sheep trample after they have fallen. From this is the poet's saying:

"Its dust raised by them like the smoke of a fire, which blazes in an old dried-up thorn-bush."

Qatāda said: It refers to the crumbling, burnt bones.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: It is the dust scattered from the walls on a windy day.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: It is what scatters from the enclosure when you strike it with sticks.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs call everything that was moist and then dried "hashīm," and from this is the poet's saying:

"You see the carcasses of the riding camels on both sides, as if their bones were dry wood of hashīm."

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the people of Lot that they denied the messengers of God, just as others had denied them, and said: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings.﴾ The explanation of "nudhur" has passed shortly before.

Then He, glorified is He, [p. 1431] explained what He punished them with, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a stone-laden storm﴾ that is, a wind which pelts them with pebbles, which are small stones.

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "al-ḥāṣib" is stones carried by the wind.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-ḥāṣib" is the fierce wind which stirs up pebbles. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with a storm like cotton-tufts scattered."

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾: We delivered them at dawn. That refers to Lot and those who followed him. "Saḥar" is the last part of the night. It has also been said that in the language of the Arabs it is the mixing of the darkness of the night with the whiteness of the beginning of the day. "Saḥar" is treated as indeterminate (and so not diptote) because it is an indefinite noun, not intending a specific dawn of a particular night; had he intended a specific one, it would have been diptote (not taking tanwīn).

Thus said al-Zajjāj, al-Akhfash, and others.

The accusative of ﴿a blessing from Us﴾ is by way of causation or as a verbal noun: that is, a favor from Us upon Lot and those who followed him. ﴿Thus do We reward those who give thanks﴾ that is, in the same manner of that reward We reward whoever gives thanks for Our blessing and does not disbelieve it.

﴿And he had already warned them of Our seizure﴾ that is, Lot warned his people of God's seizure against them, which is His severe punishment and far-reaching retribution. ﴿But they disputed about the warnings﴾ that is, they doubted the warning and did not believe him. It is the form "tafāʿalū" from "mirya," which means doubt.

﴿And they had sought to seduce him away from his guests﴾ that is, they wanted from him to let them have those who came to him from among the angels, so that they might commit lewdness with them, as is their habit. It is said: "rāwadtuhu ʿan kadhā" meaning "murāwada" and "riwād": I sought it from him; and "rāda al-kalām yarūduhu rawdan" meaning he sought it. The explanation of "murāwada" has been given in full in the surah Hūd. ﴿So We blinded their eyes﴾ that is, We made their eyes wiped smooth, with no slit visible, as the wind wipes out markers by blowing dust over them. It has also been said: God removed the light of their sight while their eyes remained in their form. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God wiped their eyes so they did not see the messengers, and so they returned. ﴿So taste My punishment and My warning﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

﴿And there came upon them in the morning a settled punishment﴾ that is, a punishment settled upon them, descending over them, not leaving them nor departing from them, came upon them at dawn.

Muqātil said: The punishment settled upon them at dawn. "Bukra" is not diptote, because it was not intended as a specific time, as was previously explained in "bi-saḥar."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ The tafsir (explanation of the Qur'an) of this has already been given in this surah. Perhaps the purpose of repeating the statement about the Qur'an being made easy for remembrance in this surah is to draw attention to the fact that it is a great favour, and no one should neglect to be grateful for it.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾, that he said: "Cold." ﴿On a day of ill omen﴾, he said: "Days of hardship."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wednesday is a day of continuous ill omen." Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him through another chain, as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ) report.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded it from Ali as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from Anas as a marfu' report, and in it: "It was said: 'How is that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Allah drowned Pharaoh and his people in it, and destroyed 'Ad and Thamud in it.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib recorded, with a chain (sanad) which al-Suyuti described as weak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The last Wednesday of the month is a day of continuous ill omen."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from them (Ibn Abbas and others), regarding ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees﴾, that he said: "The roots of the palm trees, uprooted." He said: "Uprooted."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him, also regarding the verse, that he said: "The trunks of the dark palm trees."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, regarding "and a madness (su'ur)", that he said: "Misery."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, that he said, regarding ﴿like the crushed stubble of a pen-builder﴾: "Like the burnt branches of trees used as enclosures."

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, also, regarding the verse, that he said: "Like burnt bones."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him that he said: "Like grass that is eaten by sheep."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The people of ʿĀd denied,﴾ they are the people of ʿĀd. ﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ That is: listen to how My punishment befell them and how My warning (to them) was. "Nudhur" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "warning (indhār)," as its verification has already passed. The interrogative is for expressing awe and magnitude.

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind,﴾ this clause explains what was previously stated in summary of the punishment. "Ṣarṣar" means intense cold: that is, a wind of intense cold. It has also been said that "ṣarṣar" means intense sound. Its explanation has already passed in the surah Ḥā Mīm (al-Sajda). ﴿On a day of continuous ill omen,﴾ that is, a day of constant misfortune, whose ill fortune persisted over them. They used to consider that day ominous.

Al-Zajjaj said: It has been said that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿a day of ill omen﴾ with the noun "yawm" in construct with "naḥs," and with the ḥāʾ sukūn (unvocalized). This is either the construction of a described noun with its description (iḍāfat al-mawṣūf ilā al-ṣifa), or it is by presuming an omitted noun, that is: "on the day of the punishment of an ill omen."

Al-Ḥasan read "yawmin" with tanwīn, so that "naḥsin" is its attribute (ṣifa).

Hārūn read it with a kasra on the ḥāʾ.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That day was bitter for them.

Likewise al-Kisāʾī narrated from some people that they said: it is from "marāra" (bitterness). It has also been said that it is from "mirra" meaning strength: that is, on a day of powerful, firmly established ill omen, like a thing tightly twisted that cannot be undone. The apparent meaning is that it is from "istimrār" (continuance), not from "marāra" nor from "mirra": that is, the punishment continued over them on that day until it destroyed them, and its destruction encompassed their great and small alike.

The clause ﴿uprooting people﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), either as an attribute of "rīḥan" or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. It is also permissible that it is a resumptive new clause (isti'nāf): that is, it uproots them from the earth from beneath their feet, like the uprooting of a palm tree from its root.

Mujahid said: It would uproot them from the earth and then hurl them upon their heads, breaking their necks and separating their heads from their bodies. It has also been said: it uproots the people from their houses. It has also been said: from their graves, because they had dug trenches and entered them.

﴿As if they were trunks of hollowed palm trees.﴾ "Aʿjāz" is the plural of "ʿajuz," which is the rear part of a thing. "Munqaʿir" means uprooted, torn from its root. It is said: "qaʿʿartu al-nakhla" when I uprooted the palm tree from its root until it falls. He likened them in the height of their statures, when the wind felled them and cast them on their faces, to fallen palm trees on the ground which have no heads; because the wind first tore off their heads, then overturned them on their faces. The masculine form "munqaʿir" with "aʿjāz nakhl," which is feminine, is in consideration of the wording; it is also permissible to make it feminine in consideration of the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. Al-Mubarrad said: Whatever comes to you of this type, if you wish, you may refer it to the wording by using the masculine, or to the meaning by using the feminine.

It has been said that "nakhl" and "nakhīl" may be treated as masculine or feminine.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has been given shortly before. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the denial of ʿĀd, He followed it with the denial of Thamūd, and said: ﴿Thamūd denied the warnings.﴾ It is permissible that it is the plural of "nadhīr" (warner): that is, they denied the messengers sent to them. It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun meaning "warning": that is, they denied the warning with which they were warned. Their denial of their messenger, who was Ṣāliḥ, was a denial of (all) messengers, because whoever denies one of the prophets has denied all of them, since they agree on the call to the universal principles of the laws.

﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, how could we follow a human being of our own kind, alone, with no one following him in what he calls to?

The majority read "basharan" with a naṣb (accusative), by way of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with the object pronoun): that is, "Shall we follow a single human?"

Abu al-Simāk, al-Dānī, Abu al-Ashhab, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read it with a raf (nominative) by way of ibtidāʾ (the nominal sentence beginning): "wāḥidan" is its attribute, and "nattabiʿuhu" is its predicate.

It is narrated from Abu al-Simāk that he read "basharun" with raf and "wāḥidan" with naṣb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿Indeed, then we would be in error,﴾ that is: indeed, if we followed him we would be in mistake, going astray from the truth and in "suʿur": that is, torment, hardship, and distress. Thus said al-Farrāʾ and others.

Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of "saʿīr," which is the flame of fire; and "suʿur" is madness, for it goes, such and such, due to what he burns with of heat.

Mujahid said: "suʿur" means: and distance from the truth.

Al-Suddī said: in burning. It has also been said that what is meant here is madness, from their saying: "a she-camel that is maswūra," meaning as if she were mad from the intensity of her vigor. From this is the poet's saying describing a she-camel:

"You imagine in her madness when the madness shakes her, a gait and a rhythm of travel that is tiring."

Then they repeated the denial and the disbelief, and said: 25 – ﴿Has the message been cast upon him from among us?﴾ That is: how was he singled out from among us for revelation and prophethood, when among us is one more deserving of that than him?

Then they turned away from denial and moved on to a firm assertion that he was a liar and insolent, and said: ﴿Rather, he is a liar, insolent.﴾ "Al-Ashar" means exuberance and vigor, or arrogance and haughtiness. Explaining it as arrogance and haughtiness is more fitting to the context. From this is the poet's saying:

"You became arrogant by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, and before that you did not know who conquered the villages."

The majority read "ushira" in the pattern of "fariḥa" (ushira). Abu Qilāba and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a fatḥa on the shīn and shadda on the rāʾ, as an elative form (ism tafḍīl). Al-Kisāʾī transmitted from Mujahid that he read it with a ḍamma on the shīn and a fatḥa on the hamza.

Then He, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent.﴾ What is meant by "tomorrow" is the time of the descent of the punishment upon them in this world, or the Day of Resurrection, following the custom of people in expressing the future matter by "tomorrow," even if it is distant, as in their saying: "Indeed, with today is tomorrow," and as in the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:

From this is the saying of Abu al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

"Ah, give me to drink before the wailing of the mourners, and before the agitation of the soul within the ribs, and before tomorrow, O woe to my soul over tomorrow, when my companions depart and I am not returning."

The majority read "sayaʿlamūna" with the yāʾ (third person), as a report from God, glorified is He, to Ṣāliḥ about the occurrence of the punishment upon them after a period.

Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza read it with the tāʾ (second person), as an address from Ṣāliḥ to his people.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿The people of ʿĀd denied,﴾ they are the people of ʿĀd. ﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ That is: listen to how My punishment befell them and how My warning (to them) was. "Nudhur" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "warning (indhār)," as its verification has already passed. The interrogative is for expressing awe and magnitude.

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind,﴾ this clause explains what was previously stated in summary of the punishment. "Ṣarṣar" means intense cold: that is, a wind of intense cold. It has also been said that "ṣarṣar" means intense sound. Its explanation has already passed in the surah Ḥā Mīm (al-Sajda). ﴿On a day of continuous ill omen,﴾ that is, a day of constant misfortune, whose ill fortune persisted over them. They used to consider that day ominous.

Al-Zajjaj said: It has been said that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿a day of ill omen﴾ with the noun "yawm" in construct with "naḥs," and with the ḥāʾ sukūn (unvocalized). This is either the construction of a described noun with its description (iḍāfat al-mawṣūf ilā al-ṣifa), or it is by presuming an omitted noun, that is: "on the day of the punishment of an ill omen."

Al-Ḥasan read "yawmin" with tanwīn, so that "naḥsin" is its attribute (ṣifa).

Hārūn read it with a kasra on the ḥāʾ.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That day was bitter for them.

Likewise al-Kisāʾī narrated from some people that they said: it is from "marāra" (bitterness). It has also been said that it is from "mirra" meaning strength: that is, on a day of powerful, firmly established ill omen, like a thing tightly twisted that cannot be undone. The apparent meaning is that it is from "istimrār" (continuance), not from "marāra" nor from "mirra": that is, the punishment continued over them on that day until it destroyed them, and its destruction encompassed their great and small alike.

The clause ﴿uprooting people﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), either as an attribute of "rīḥan" or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. It is also permissible that it is a resumptive new clause (isti'nāf): that is, it uproots them from the earth from beneath their feet, like the uprooting of a palm tree from its root.

Mujahid said: It would uproot them from the earth and then hurl them upon their heads, breaking their necks and separating their heads from their bodies. It has also been said: it uproots the people from their houses. It has also been said: from their graves, because they had dug trenches and entered them.

﴿As if they were trunks of hollowed palm trees.﴾ "Aʿjāz" is the plural of "ʿajuz," which is the rear part of a thing. "Munqaʿir" means uprooted, torn from its root. It is said: "qaʿʿartu al-nakhla" when I uprooted the palm tree from its root until it falls. He likened them in the height of their statures, when the wind felled them and cast them on their faces, to fallen palm trees on the ground which have no heads; because the wind first tore off their heads, then overturned them on their faces. The masculine form "munqaʿir" with "aʿjāz nakhl," which is feminine, is in consideration of the wording; it is also permissible to make it feminine in consideration of the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. Al-Mubarrad said: Whatever comes to you of this type, if you wish, you may refer it to the wording by using the masculine, or to the meaning by using the feminine.

It has been said that "nakhl" and "nakhīl" may be treated as masculine or feminine.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has been given shortly before. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the denial of ʿĀd, He followed it with the denial of Thamūd, and said: ﴿Thamūd denied the warnings.﴾ It is permissible that it is the plural of "nadhīr" (warner): that is, they denied the messengers sent to them. It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun meaning "warning": that is, they denied the warning with which they were warned. Their denial of their messenger, who was Ṣāliḥ, was a denial of (all) messengers, because whoever denies one of the prophets has denied all of them, since they agree on the call to the universal principles of the laws.

﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, how could we follow a human being of our own kind, alone, with no one following him in what he calls to?

The majority read "basharan" with a naṣb (accusative), by way of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with the object pronoun): that is, "Shall we follow a single human?"

Abu al-Simāk, al-Dānī, Abu al-Ashhab, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read it with a raf (nominative) by way of ibtidāʾ (the nominal sentence beginning): "wāḥidan" is its attribute, and "nattabiʿuhu" is its predicate.

It is narrated from Abu al-Simāk that he read "basharun" with raf and "wāḥidan" with naṣb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿Indeed, then we would be in error,﴾ that is: indeed, if we followed him we would be in mistake, going astray from the truth and in "suʿur": that is, torment, hardship, and distress. Thus said al-Farrāʾ and others.

Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of "saʿīr," which is the flame of fire; and "suʿur" is madness, for it goes, such and such, due to what he burns with of heat.

Mujahid said: "suʿur" means: and distance from the truth.

Al-Suddī said: in burning. It has also been said that what is meant here is madness, from their saying: "a she-camel that is maswūra," meaning as if she were mad from the intensity of her vigor. From this is the poet's saying describing a she-camel:

"You imagine in her madness when the madness shakes her, a gait and a rhythm of travel that is tiring."

Then they repeated the denial and the disbelief, and said: 25 – ﴿Has the message been cast upon him from among us?﴾ That is: how was he singled out from among us for revelation and prophethood, when among us is one more deserving of that than him?

Then they turned away from denial and moved on to a firm assertion that he was a liar and insolent, and said: ﴿Rather, he is a liar, insolent.﴾ "Al-Ashar" means exuberance and vigor, or arrogance and haughtiness. Explaining it as arrogance and haughtiness is more fitting to the context. From this is the poet's saying:

"You became arrogant by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, and before that you did not know who conquered the villages."

The majority read "ushira" in the pattern of "fariḥa" (ushira). Abu Qilāba and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a fatḥa on the shīn and shadda on the rāʾ, as an elative form (ism tafḍīl). Al-Kisāʾī transmitted from Mujahid that he read it with a ḍamma on the shīn and a fatḥa on the hamza.

Then He, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent.﴾ What is meant by "tomorrow" is the time of the descent of the punishment upon them in this world, or the Day of Resurrection, following the custom of people in expressing the future matter by "tomorrow," even if it is distant, as in their saying: "Indeed, with today is tomorrow," and as in the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:

"For death in it are arrows that never miss; whoever has not died today will die tomorrow."

From this is the saying of Abu al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

"Ah, give me to drink before the wailing of the mourners, and before the agitation of the soul within the ribs, and before tomorrow, O woe to my soul over tomorrow, when my companions depart and I am not returning."

The majority read "sayaʿlamūna" with the yāʾ (third person), as a report from God, glorified is He, to Ṣāliḥ about the occurrence of the punishment upon them after a period.

Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza read it with the tāʾ (second person), as an address from Ṣāliḥ to his people.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾ is a resumptive new sentence explaining what was previously stated in summary of the threat: that is, indeed We are bringing her out from the rock according to what they proposed. ﴿As a trial for them﴾ that is, a test and examination. The accusative of "fitna" is by way of causation (ʿilla). "So watch them" means: wait and see what they do, and be patient over what harm reaches you from them.

﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them﴾ that is, between Thamūd and the she-camel: a day for her, and a day for them, as in His saying: ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 155]. He said "nabbi'hum" with the pronoun for rational beings, by way of precedence (taghlīb). ﴿Every drink shall be attended.﴾ "Shirb" with a kasra on the shīn means the allotted share of water. The meaning of "muḥtaḍar" (attended) is that the one entitled to it attends it: so the she-camel attends it on one day, and they attend it on another day.

Mujahid said: Thamūd would come to the water on their turn day, and drink, and they would come on her turn day and milk her.

The majority read "qisma" with a kasra on the qāf, in the sense of "maqsūm" (allotted). Abu ʿAmr, in a transmission from him, read it with a fatḥa.

﴿Then they called their companion﴾ that is, Thamūd called their companion, who was Qidār ibn Sālif, the hamstringer of the she-camel, urging him to hamstring her. ﴿So he took it in hand and hamstrung her.﴾ That is, he took hold of the she-camel and hamstrung her; or he dared to undertake the means of hamstringing and so hamstrung her. "Taʿāṭā" means taking hold of a thing with effort.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: He lay in ambush for her beneath a tree on her path, and shot her with an arrow which pierced the muscle of her leg; then he attacked her with the sword, cut her hamstring, and then slaughtered her.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He explained the punishment which He had mentioned in summary, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry,﴾ ʿAṭāʾ said: He means the cry of Gabriel. Its explanation has passed in the surah Hūd and in al-Aʿrāf. ﴿So they became like the crushed remains of a fence-builder's enclosure.﴾ The majority read "al-muḥtaẓir" with a kasra on the ẓāʾ. "Hashīm" means the debris and dried part of trees; "al-muḥtaẓir" is the owner of an enclosure, the one who makes for his sheep an enclosure to protect them from the cold wind. It is said: "iḥtaẓara ʿalā ghanamihi" when he gathered trees and placed some of them upon others.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-muḥtaẓir" is the one who builds the enclosure.

Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Abu al-ʿĀliya read it with a fatḥa on the ẓāʾ: that is, like the crushed remains of the enclosure. So whoever reads with a kasra intends the agent of the enclosing; whoever reads with a fatḥa intends the enclosure, which is a "faʿīla" in the sense of "mafʿūla" (passive). The meaning of the verse is that they became like trees which dry out in the enclosure and which the sheep trample after they have fallen. From this is the poet's saying:

"Its dust raised by them like the smoke of a fire, which blazes in an old dried-up thorn-bush."

Qatāda said: It refers to the crumbling, burnt bones.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: It is the dust scattered from the walls on a windy day.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: It is what scatters from the enclosure when you strike it with sticks.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs call everything that was moist and then dried "hashīm," and from this is the poet's saying:

"You see the carcasses of the riding camels on both sides, as if their bones were dry wood of hashīm."

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the people of Lot that they denied the messengers of God, just as others had denied them, and said: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings.﴾ The explanation of "nudhur" has passed shortly before.

Then He, glorified is He, [p. 1431] explained what He punished them with, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a stone-laden storm﴾ that is, a wind which pelts them with pebbles, which are small stones.

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "al-ḥāṣib" is stones carried by the wind.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-ḥāṣib" is the fierce wind which stirs up pebbles. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with a storm like cotton-tufts scattered."

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾: We delivered them at dawn. That refers to Lot and those who followed him. "Saḥar" is the last part of the night. It has also been said that in the language of the Arabs it is the mixing of the darkness of the night with the whiteness of the beginning of the day. "Saḥar" is treated as indeterminate (and so not diptote) because it is an indefinite noun, not intending a specific dawn of a particular night; had he intended a specific one, it would have been diptote (not taking tanwīn).

Thus said al-Zajjāj, al-Akhfash, and others.

The accusative of ﴿a blessing from Us﴾ is by way of causation or as a verbal noun: that is, a favor from Us upon Lot and those who followed him. ﴿Thus do We reward those who give thanks﴾ that is, in the same manner of that reward We reward whoever gives thanks for Our blessing and does not disbelieve it.

﴿And he had already warned them of Our seizure﴾ that is, Lot warned his people of God's seizure against them, which is His severe punishment and far-reaching retribution. ﴿But they disputed about the warnings﴾ that is, they doubted the warning and did not believe him. It is the form "tafāʿalū" from "mirya," which means doubt.

﴿And they had sought to seduce him away from his guests﴾ that is, they wanted from him to let them have those who came to him from among the angels, so that they might commit lewdness with them, as is their habit. It is said: "rāwadtuhu ʿan kadhā" meaning "murāwada" and "riwād": I sought it from him; and "rāda al-kalām yarūduhu rawdan" meaning he sought it. The explanation of "murāwada" has been given in full in the surah Hūd. ﴿So We blinded their eyes﴾ that is, We made their eyes wiped smooth, with no slit visible, as the wind wipes out markers by blowing dust over them. It has also been said: God removed the light of their sight while their eyes remained in their form. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God wiped their eyes so they did not see the messengers, and so they returned. ﴿So taste My punishment and My warning﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

﴿And there came upon them in the morning a settled punishment﴾ that is, a punishment settled upon them, descending over them, not leaving them nor departing from them, came upon them at dawn.

Muqātil said: The punishment settled upon them at dawn. "Bukra" is not diptote, because it was not intended as a specific time, as was previously explained in "bi-saḥar."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ The tafsir (explanation of the Qur'an) of this has already been given in this surah. Perhaps the purpose of repeating the statement about the Qur'an being made easy for remembrance in this surah is to draw attention to the fact that it is a great favour, and no one should neglect to be grateful for it.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾, that he said: "Cold." ﴿On a day of ill omen﴾, he said: "Days of hardship."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wednesday is a day of continuous ill omen." Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him through another chain, as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ) report.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded it from Ali as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from Anas as a marfu' report, and in it: "It was said: 'How is that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Allah drowned Pharaoh and his people in it, and destroyed 'Ad and Thamud in it.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib recorded, with a chain (sanad) which al-Suyuti described as weak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The last Wednesday of the month is a day of continuous ill omen."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from them (Ibn Abbas and others), regarding ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees﴾, that he said: "The roots of the palm trees, uprooted." He said: "Uprooted."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him, also regarding the verse, that he said: "The trunks of the dark palm trees."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, regarding "and a madness (su'ur)", that he said: "Misery."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, that he said, regarding ﴿like the crushed stubble of a pen-builder﴾: "Like the burnt branches of trees used as enclosures."

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, also, regarding the verse, that he said: "Like burnt bones."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him that he said: "Like grass that is eaten by sheep."

﴿Then they called their companion﴾ that is, Thamūd called their companion, who was Qidār ibn Sālif, the hamstringer of the she-camel, urging him to hamstring her. ﴿So he took it in hand and hamstrung her.﴾ That is, he took hold of the she-camel and hamstrung her; or he dared to undertake the means of hamstringing and so hamstrung her. "Taʿāṭā" means taking hold of a thing with effort.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq said: He lay in ambush for her beneath a tree on her path, and shot her with an arrow which pierced the muscle of her leg; then he attacked her with the sword, cut her hamstring, and then slaughtered her.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He explained the punishment which He had mentioned in summary, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single cry,﴾ ʿAṭāʾ said: He means the cry of Gabriel. Its explanation has passed in the surah Hūd and in al-Aʿrāf. ﴿So they became like the crushed remains of a fence-builder's enclosure.﴾ The majority read "al-muḥtaẓir" with a kasra on the ẓāʾ. "Hashīm" means the debris and dried part of trees; "al-muḥtaẓir" is the owner of an enclosure, the one who makes for his sheep an enclosure to protect them from the cold wind. It is said: "iḥtaẓara ʿalā ghanamihi" when he gathered trees and placed some of them upon others.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-muḥtaẓir" is the one who builds the enclosure.

Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Abu al-ʿĀliya read it with a fatḥa on the ẓāʾ: that is, like the crushed remains of the enclosure. So whoever reads with a kasra intends the agent of the enclosing; whoever reads with a fatḥa intends the enclosure, which is a "faʿīla" in the sense of "mafʿūla" (passive). The meaning of the verse is that they became like trees which dry out in the enclosure and which the sheep trample after they have fallen. From this is the poet's saying:

"Its dust raised by them like the smoke of a fire, which blazes in an old dried-up thorn-bush."

Qatāda said: It refers to the crumbling, burnt bones.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: It is the dust scattered from the walls on a windy day.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: It is what scatters from the enclosure when you strike it with sticks.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs call everything that was moist and then dried "hashīm," and from this is the poet's saying:

"You see the carcasses of the riding camels on both sides, as if their bones were dry wood of hashīm."

﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the people of Lot that they denied the messengers of God, just as others had denied them, and said: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings.﴾ The explanation of "nudhur" has passed shortly before.

Then He, glorified is He, [p. 1431] explained what He punished them with, and said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a stone-laden storm﴾ that is, a wind which pelts them with pebbles, which are small stones.

Abu ʿUbayda and al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "al-ḥāṣib" is stones carried by the wind.

Al-Ṣiḥāḥ says: "al-ḥāṣib" is the fierce wind which stirs up pebbles. From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north of Syria, it strikes them with a storm like cotton-tufts scattered."

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾: We delivered them at dawn. That refers to Lot and those who followed him. "Saḥar" is the last part of the night. It has also been said that in the language of the Arabs it is the mixing of the darkness of the night with the whiteness of the beginning of the day. "Saḥar" is treated as indeterminate (and so not diptote) because it is an indefinite noun, not intending a specific dawn of a particular night; had he intended a specific one, it would have been diptote (not taking tanwīn).

Thus said al-Zajjāj, al-Akhfash, and others.

The accusative of ﴿a blessing from Us﴾ is by way of causation or as a verbal noun: that is, a favor from Us upon Lot and those who followed him. ﴿Thus do We reward those who give thanks﴾ that is, in the same manner of that reward We reward whoever gives thanks for Our blessing and does not disbelieve it.

﴿And he had already warned them of Our seizure﴾ that is, Lot warned his people of God's seizure against them, which is His severe punishment and far-reaching retribution. ﴿But they disputed about the warnings﴾ that is, they doubted the warning and did not believe him. It is the form "tafāʿalū" from "mirya," which means doubt.

﴿And they had sought to seduce him away from his guests﴾ that is, they wanted from him to let them have those who came to him from among the angels, so that they might commit lewdness with them, as is their habit. It is said: "rāwadtuhu ʿan kadhā" meaning "murāwada" and "riwād": I sought it from him; and "rāda al-kalām yarūduhu rawdan" meaning he sought it. The explanation of "murāwada" has been given in full in the surah Hūd. ﴿So We blinded their eyes﴾ that is, We made their eyes wiped smooth, with no slit visible, as the wind wipes out markers by blowing dust over them. It has also been said: God removed the light of their sight while their eyes remained in their form. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: God wiped their eyes so they did not see the messengers, and so they returned. ﴿So taste My punishment and My warning﴾ Its explanation has passed in this surah.

﴿And there came upon them in the morning a settled punishment﴾ that is, a punishment settled upon them, descending over them, not leaving them nor departing from them, came upon them at dawn.

Muqātil said: The punishment settled upon them at dawn. "Bukra" is not diptote, because it was not intended as a specific time, as was previously explained in "bi-saḥar."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 54, verses 18–40 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So taste My punishment and warnings.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ The tafsir (explanation of the Qur'an) of this has already been given in this surah. Perhaps the purpose of repeating the statement about the Qur'an being made easy for remembrance in this surah is to draw attention to the fact that it is a great favour, and no one should neglect to be grateful for it.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) recorded from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾, that he said: "Cold." ﴿On a day of ill omen﴾, he said: "Days of hardship."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wednesday is a day of continuous ill omen." Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him through another chain, as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet ﷺ) report.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded it from Ali as a marfu' report.

Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from Anas as a marfu' report, and in it: "It was said: 'How is that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Allah drowned Pharaoh and his people in it, and destroyed 'Ad and Thamud in it.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib recorded, with a chain (sanad) which al-Suyuti described as weak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The last Wednesday of the month is a day of continuous ill omen."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from them (Ibn Abbas and others), regarding ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees﴾, that he said: "The roots of the palm trees, uprooted." He said: "Uprooted."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him, also regarding the verse, that he said: "The trunks of the dark palm trees."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, regarding "and a madness (su'ur)", that he said: "Misery."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him, also, that he said, regarding ﴿like the crushed stubble of a pen-builder﴾: "Like the burnt branches of trees used as enclosures."

Ibn Jarir recorded from him, also, regarding the verse, that he said: "Like burnt bones."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him that he said: "Like grass that is eaten by sheep."

His saying: ﴿The people of ʿĀd denied,﴾ they are the people of ʿĀd. ﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ That is: listen to how My punishment befell them and how My warning (to them) was. "Nudhur" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) meaning "warning (indhār)," as its verification has already passed. The interrogative is for expressing awe and magnitude.

﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a furious wind,﴾ this clause explains what was previously stated in summary of the punishment. "Ṣarṣar" means intense cold: that is, a wind of intense cold. It has also been said that "ṣarṣar" means intense sound. Its explanation has already passed in the surah Ḥā Mīm (al-Sajda). ﴿On a day of continuous ill omen,﴾ that is, a day of constant misfortune, whose ill fortune persisted over them. They used to consider that day ominous.

Al-Zajjaj said: It has been said that it was a Wednesday at the end of the month.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿a day of ill omen﴾ with the noun "yawm" in construct with "naḥs," and with the ḥāʾ sukūn (unvocalized). This is either the construction of a described noun with its description (iḍāfat al-mawṣūf ilā al-ṣifa), or it is by presuming an omitted noun, that is: "on the day of the punishment of an ill omen."

Al-Ḥasan read "yawmin" with tanwīn, so that "naḥsin" is its attribute (ṣifa).

Hārūn read it with a kasra on the ḥāʾ.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: That day was bitter for them.

Likewise al-Kisāʾī narrated from some people that they said: it is from "marāra" (bitterness). It has also been said that it is from "mirra" meaning strength: that is, on a day of powerful, firmly established ill omen, like a thing tightly twisted that cannot be undone. The apparent meaning is that it is from "istimrār" (continuance), not from "marāra" nor from "mirra": that is, the punishment continued over them on that day until it destroyed them, and its destruction encompassed their great and small alike.

The clause ﴿uprooting people﴾ is in a position of accusative (naṣb), either as an attribute of "rīḥan" or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. It is also permissible that it is a resumptive new clause (isti'nāf): that is, it uproots them from the earth from beneath their feet, like the uprooting of a palm tree from its root.

Mujahid said: It would uproot them from the earth and then hurl them upon their heads, breaking their necks and separating their heads from their bodies. It has also been said: it uproots the people from their houses. It has also been said: from their graves, because they had dug trenches and entered them.

﴿As if they were trunks of hollowed palm trees.﴾ "Aʿjāz" is the plural of "ʿajuz," which is the rear part of a thing. "Munqaʿir" means uprooted, torn from its root. It is said: "qaʿʿartu al-nakhla" when I uprooted the palm tree from its root until it falls. He likened them in the height of their statures, when the wind felled them and cast them on their faces, to fallen palm trees on the ground which have no heads; because the wind first tore off their heads, then overturned them on their faces. The masculine form "munqaʿir" with "aʿjāz nakhl," which is feminine, is in consideration of the wording; it is also permissible to make it feminine in consideration of the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. Al-Mubarrad said: Whatever comes to you of this type, if you wish, you may refer it to the wording by using the masculine, or to the meaning by using the feminine.

It has been said that "nakhl" and "nakhīl" may be treated as masculine or feminine.

﴿So how was My punishment and My warning?﴾ Its explanation has been given shortly before. Likewise His saying: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will take heed?﴾

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned the denial of ʿĀd, He followed it with the denial of Thamūd, and said: ﴿Thamūd denied the warnings.﴾ It is permissible that it is the plural of "nadhīr" (warner): that is, they denied the messengers sent to them. It is also permissible that it is a verbal noun meaning "warning": that is, they denied the warning with which they were warned. Their denial of their messenger, who was Ṣāliḥ, was a denial of (all) messengers, because whoever denies one of the prophets has denied all of them, since they agree on the call to the universal principles of the laws.

﴿So they said: "Shall we follow a single human being from among us?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial: that is, how could we follow a human being of our own kind, alone, with no one following him in what he calls to?

The majority read "basharan" with a naṣb (accusative), by way of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with the object pronoun): that is, "Shall we follow a single human?"

Abu al-Simāk, al-Dānī, Abu al-Ashhab, and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ read it with a raf (nominative) by way of ibtidāʾ (the nominal sentence beginning): "wāḥidan" is its attribute, and "nattabiʿuhu" is its predicate.

It is narrated from Abu al-Simāk that he read "basharun" with raf and "wāḥidan" with naṣb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿Indeed, then we would be in error,﴾ that is: indeed, if we followed him we would be in mistake, going astray from the truth and in "suʿur": that is, torment, hardship, and distress. Thus said al-Farrāʾ and others.

Abu ʿUbayda said: it is the plural of "saʿīr," which is the flame of fire; and "suʿur" is madness, for it goes, such and such, due to what he burns with of heat.

Mujahid said: "suʿur" means: and distance from the truth.

Al-Suddī said: in burning. It has also been said that what is meant here is madness, from their saying: "a she-camel that is maswūra," meaning as if she were mad from the intensity of her vigor. From this is the poet's saying describing a she-camel:

"You imagine in her madness when the madness shakes her, a gait and a rhythm of travel that is tiring."

Then they repeated the denial and the disbelief, and said: 25 – ﴿Has the message been cast upon him from among us?﴾ That is: how was he singled out from among us for revelation and prophethood, when among us is one more deserving of that than him?

Then they turned away from denial and moved on to a firm assertion that he was a liar and insolent, and said: ﴿Rather, he is a liar, insolent.﴾ "Al-Ashar" means exuberance and vigor, or arrogance and haughtiness. Explaining it as arrogance and haughtiness is more fitting to the context. From this is the poet's saying:

"You became arrogant by wearing silk brocade, when you put it on, and before that you did not know who conquered the villages."

The majority read "ushira" in the pattern of "fariḥa" (ushira). Abu Qilāba and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a fatḥa on the shīn and shadda on the rāʾ, as an elative form (ism tafḍīl). Al-Kisāʾī transmitted from Mujahid that he read it with a ḍamma on the shīn and a fatḥa on the hamza.

Then He, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent.﴾ What is meant by "tomorrow" is the time of the descent of the punishment upon them in this world, or the Day of Resurrection, following the custom of people in expressing the future matter by "tomorrow," even if it is distant, as in their saying: "Indeed, with today is tomorrow," and as in the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾa:

"For death in it are arrows that never miss; whoever has not died today will die tomorrow."

From this is the saying of Abu al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

"Ah, give me to drink before the wailing of the mourners, and before the agitation of the soul within the ribs, and before tomorrow, O woe to my soul over tomorrow, when my companions depart and I am not returning."

The majority read "sayaʿlamūna" with the yāʾ (third person), as a report from God, glorified is He, to Ṣāliḥ about the occurrence of the punishment upon them after a period.

Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza read it with the tāʾ (second person), as an address from Ṣāliḥ to his people.

The clause ﴿Indeed, We are sending the she-camel﴾ is a resumptive new sentence explaining what was previously stated in summary of the threat: that is, indeed We are bringing her out from the rock according to what they proposed. ﴿As a trial for them﴾ that is, a test and examination. The accusative of "fitna" is by way of causation (ʿilla). "So watch them" means: wait and see what they do, and be patient over what harm reaches you from them.

﴿And inform them that the water is to be shared between them﴾ that is, between Thamūd and the she-camel: a day for her, and a day for them, as in His saying: ﴿For her is a drink, and for you is a drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 155].
